For once, things were moving fast in the nation's capital.Washington was hosting an IndyCar race through its streets Sunday, with President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump kicking off the Freedom 250 Grand Prix by leading a slow lap in the presidential limousine through the course. Soon after, the president waved the green flag to start the race and drivers began whipping through downtown, including a stretch along Pennsylvania Avenue not too far from the White House.“I’m going to make a little circle in a nice, secure car, slightly slower than the ones we’re going to witness, but we’re going to have fun,” Trump said in an interview on Fox shortly before the ride.The open-wheel race, with cars whizzing past Washington’s monuments at speeds approaching 200 mph, is the latest of Trump’s celebrations this year to mark America’s 250th birthday.Trump’s other events to mark the semiquincentennial of the Declaration of Independence’s signing have included a UFC fight on the White House lawn, military aircraft flyovers, a massive July Fourth fireworks show on the National Mall and a Great American State Fair that the president headlined after scores of ’90s-era musical acts dropped out. The events have all had a Trumpian flair, featuring appearances from his friends and the aim of showcasing spectacle, Americana and power.In this latest case, it was be horsepower.Racing day brings out some of Trump's favoritesSunday included some of Trump's favorite flourishes. One of his favorite singers, tenor Christopher Macchio, performed, “The Star-Spangled Banner.” A trained bald eagle was dramatically released near the start line, and it swooped and flew overhead before returning to its handler.There were flyovers of military aircraft, which have boomed over the city during the July Fourth celebrations, among other events. One flyover Sunday involved a formation featuring a B-2 stealth bomber, which Trump frequently boasts about for its role in dropping massive bunker-buster bombs on Iranian nuclear facilities last year.Air Force One, escorted by four fighter jets, flew overhead as Trump did his lap. The jet was the Qatar-gifted aircraft that the president has been using as Air Force One, which has attracted scrutiny not only for Trump’s acceptance of the luxury gift but because it is not equipped with some of the same missile detection and countermeasure systems found on older presidential jets.The IndyCar race took place Trump has struggled to resolve the war he started nearly six months ago with Iran, a conflict that has driven up gasoline prices and exacerbated worries from officials in his Republican Party that voters in this November’s midterm elections see the president as distracted and not focused enough on cost-of-living concerns.Trump in his second term has increasingly seemed to focus on relishing the presidency’s ceremonial aspects. That's included a healthy dose of visits to sporting events — including an appearance last month at the World Cup final, where he presented the trophy to winner Spain and lingered onstage with the team as its members jumped in a hail of confetti.Bringing Indy to DC was a longtime quest for racing series ownerFrom his viewing box, Trump had the honor of waving the green flag to kick off the race.Before the race, Trump and his wife met and chatted with some of the race drivers. They then took a slow drive through the course in a small motorcade and could be seen waving at the crowd as a Marine Corps band played “Stars and Stripes Forever."IndyCar series owner Roger Penske, a longtime friend of Trump’s who received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from him in 2019, helped lead the effort to bring the race to Washington.Trump told Fox on Sunday that Penske told him that he had been trying to bring the race to Washington for 20 years.“When he came to see Trump it got done in about 15 minutes and it’s turned out to be much bigger than we ever even thought possible,” the president said, referring to himself in the third person.Penske met Trump when he arrived at the course and later joined him in his viewing box, as did the president’s friend and UFC CEO Dana White, who helped put on the fight at the White House in June.An executive order Trump signed earlier this year calling for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix declared that the “cars and drivers inspire awe and respect in all who watch this quintessentially American sport,” and the event will “showcase the majesty of our great city as drivers navigate a track around our iconic national monuments in celebration of America’s 250th birthday.”Trump wanted to hear ‘freedom roar’ from the powerful racing machines“Their beautiful cars are going to make freedom roar. This will be a freedom that’s roaring like never before,” Trump said at the White House earlier this month as he promoted the event.Bud Denker, president of Penske Corporation and the race’s chair, said that Penske is paying for the “vast majority” of the race, including building the track and road improvements, while the District of Columbia handled some repaving.Among the changes needed on the city’s streets for the Indycar race was the welding of more than 200 maintenance hole covers to ensure the race cars don’t suck them up off the road.Sunday’s festivities were also the latest opportunity for Trump to revel in the way he’s putting his mark on the nation’s capital, including large banners showing his face on government buildings, the construction of a massive White House ballroom, a gold-adorned Oval Office and botched repairs at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The reason why I brought you here is because I cover this area. Lucie County is home to me. It is so special."WATCH: What I learned during my visit really stuck with me. Al's Family Farm has been run by the same family since 1977 – the Schorner family – which means you're guaranteed fresh and real produce. In fact, I discovered that 9 out of 10 so-called gift fruit companies don't even own a packinghouse! But you can trust Al's to pick, pack and ship your citrus from the family itself.Now, Brooke had something special planned for me— indulging in a Sunshine Shake.But before I could get my hands on that famous Sunshine Shake, Brooke had other plans: Trying a Georgia peach.And let me tell you, I didn't even wait for permission. That peach was incredible, but I was getting excited about the shake that everyone was talking about.This hot and humid day was perfect for a Sunshine Shake. "Oh my goodness, that is so fresh," I exclaimed after my first sip.But here's what made this visit even more meaningful. Brooke reminded me of something important- "If you ate today, thank a farmer." Farmers play such an important role in all of our lives, and we don't always think about the people who worked hard to produce the food we enjoy.I was so thankful for my trip to Al's Family Farm. It reminded me that some of the best experiences happen when you slow down, appreciate where your food comes from, and connect with the hardworking families who make it all possible.

A suspect has been identified and faces charges in connection with a deadly shooting that happened in Fort Pierce earlier this summer. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The Fort Pierce Police Department announced that 28-year-old Cornelius Trevon Ivory was identified as the suspect in a homicide that occurred July 5 on South 14th Street. He is facing charges of first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder, possession of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. A 28-year-old woman sustained a non-life-threatening injury to her hand, while a 28-year-old man sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was transported to a local hospital. The police department announced on July 7 that the man died from his injuries. An initial investigation revealed that the victims were involved in an earlier altercation at the 5800 block of Okeechobee Road before returning to their residence. As the victims arrived home, a man not believed to be involved in the altercation on Okeechobee Road, approached them and fired a weapon before leaving the area. Detectives said they developed probable cause for Ivory's arrest through an extensive investigation that included eyewitness accounts, information from community members, law enforcement databases and assistance from the Palm Bay Police Department. Fort Pierce Police obtained an arrest warrant charging Ivory in connection with the killing. Authorities said he was served with an arrest warrant while in the St. Lucie County Jail involving possession of weapon by a convicted felon on July 24. Ivory remains in the jail, and his first appearance in the latest case was Friday. Investigators credited members of the public who came forward with information during the case, as well as the Palm Bay Police Department for assisting in the investigation. The investigation remains active. Anyone with additional information is encouraged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Congressman Brian Mast is pointing to progress on some of the Treasure Coast’s biggest issues as he campaigns for a sixth term, while laying out what he says still needs to be done on taxes, transportation, water quality, and health concerns. In a wide-ranging one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, the Republican congressman discussed everything from Lake Okeechobee and Brightline to Florida’s rapid growth and concerns about a possible cancer cluster in St. The interview is part of CBS12 News’ continuing coverage of the race for Florida’s 21st Congressional District . CBS12 News had hoped to bring voters a debate between the Republican and Democratic nominees, but the Democratic primary remained too close to call for days. It was not until Friday that the Associated Press declared James Martin the winner by a little more than 300 votes. CBS12 News will sit down one-on-one with Martin next Friday to give voters a chance to hear directly from Mast’s Democratic opponent ahead of the November election. See also: James Martin wins Democratic primary, will face Brian Mast in Florida’s 21st District Mast, who has represented the area since 2017, said one of the accomplishments he is most proud of is the progress made toward reducing harmful Lake Okeechobee discharges into the St. He pointed to changes in the way the Army Corps of Engineers manages Lake Okeechobee, the construction of the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir, and increased federal funding for Everglades restoration. Mast said federal funding for ecosystem restoration has grown from roughly $60 million to $65 million a year when he entered office to hundreds of millions of dollars annually. He said those projects have helped dramatically reduce the threat of damaging discharges into the Treasure Coast’s waterways. I hope they look at it and they say, you know what? In 2016, when Brian Mast came into office, or before he came into office, we couldn't go and sit on our dock in our backyard because there were toxic algal blooms all around St. Lucie, all across the Treasure Coast, Mast said. Brightline station on the Treasure Coast Mast also said he wants Treasure Coast residents to get more benefit from Brightline trains that currently travel through the region without stopping. Absolutely, Mast said when asked whether he would like to see a Brightline presence on the Treasure Coast. If they're going to be instead of just a pass through through our community, a place where people can get on and get off, that would be a benefit. But Mast questioned whether taxpayers should be expected to shoulder the full cost of a new station. He said Brightline has sought public funding for a station that could cost tens of millions of dollars and suggested a less expensive passenger platform should at least be considered. Mast also highlighted roughly $220 million in funding for replacement of the aging Florida East Coast Railway bridge over the St. The new bridge is expected to provide significantly more clearance for boats, reducing conflicts between rail and marine traffic. Renewed push for cancer cluster investigation Mast also told CBS12 News he has asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to take another look at concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. The aggressive form of brain cancer has raised concerns among some families who believe the number of cases in the area warrants additional investigation. Previous state and federal reviews did not determine that a cancer cluster existed. Mast said the emergence of additional cases deserves another examination. I have requested again that the CDC come in, Mast said. We're seeing more instances of this aggressive brain tumor. You need to come in and you need to take a look. Mast said he wants federal health officials to provide residents with detailed data explaining how the cases were evaluated and whether there is any connection between them. Supporting Amendment 3 Mast also gave his full support to Amendment 3, which would increase Florida’s homestead exemption and reduce property taxes for qualifying homeowners. For Mast, the issue comes down to allowing Floridians to keep more of their money. I fully support reducing the tax burden, Mast said. Every dollar that we spend in government, at any level of government, federal or local, it comes out of your pocket. Cities, counties, and some public safety agencies have warned the amendment could reduce the money available to provide local services. Mast acknowledged there could be an impact on local budgets but said governments should also examine their own spending and look for places to cut. There are absolutely places that our cities and our counties can cut, Mast said. Growth and data centers With Port St. Lucie County experiencing explosive population growth, Mast said federal infrastructure funding will be an important part of keeping up. As a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, Mast said his role allows him to advocate for federal dollars for roads, bridges, airports and other major projects in the district. He also weighed in on the growing debate over massive data centers needed to power artificial intelligence and other technology. Mast acknowledged the country needs data centers but said that does not mean they need to be built in South Florida. Do they need to be in your backyard or in the 21st congressional district? Absolutely not, Mast said. He said those decisions ultimately belong to local communities, which have to weigh potential jobs and tax revenue against demands on electricity, water and the character of the community. Health care and affordability On health care, Mast said he does not support bringing back enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that were tied to the COVID-19 pandemic. Instead, he pointed to efforts to reduce prescription drug prices and said consumers should have more flexibility to choose health plans based on what they actually need. Mast also argued that reducing taxes is one of the most effective ways Washington can address affordability, pointing to tax reductions involving tips, overtime and Social Security. Iran and gas prices As chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Mast also defended the U.S. Mast argued Iran has targeted American interests and service members for years and said preventing the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon is critical to U.S. He acknowledged that instability in the Middle East has contributed to higher gas prices and said he supports eliminating the federal gasoline and diesel taxes as another way to lower prices at the pump. Term limits Despite seeking a sixth term himself, Mast said he supports congressional term limits and has signed a pledge committing to vote for them if legislation reaches the House floor. If he were writing the proposal, Mast said he would limit House members to three terms, or six years, while allowing one or possibly two Senate terms. Mast said his own record is what he wants voters to consider as he asks them for another term particularly his work on the Treasure Coast’s waterways, veterans, and taxes. I hope they say, you know what, Brian does what he says, Mast said.

Lucie man faces multiple charges involving a minor after officers served a search warrant at a home Thursday morning, authorities said. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. at a residence in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. During the operation, officers arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz without incident Police said Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. The response drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Authorities said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry into the home. "It's a diversion to either make entry. When conducting a high-risk operation, these are utilized just for the safety of both the officers and the individual," police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation and say they are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active. "As a father of three myself, we take it very serious anytime there is a child involved," Martinez said. Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. Lucie voters are deciding Tuesday who they want to lead one of Florida's largest cities, with growth, traffic, development and the future of the city among the major issues in the mayoral race. CBS12 News sat down with incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin and challengers Steven Giordano and Eric Strazzeri ahead of Election Day, asking them the same questions about some of the biggest concerns facing Port St. Lucie and what they would do if elected. Their answers reveal different approaches to managing a city that continues to grow. Lucie's growth Giordano said he believes the city needs to slow development and focus on whether existing infrastructure can handle what is already being built. "I want to slow down the growth and make sure that our infrastructure can handle what we already have," Giordano said. He said the city needs to make sure its drainage systems, roads and traffic infrastructure can keep up with development. Giordano also said he wants the city to focus more heavily on supporting local businesses and attracting higher-paying jobs. Martin said one challenge is that many development rights were granted decades ago and cannot simply be taken away by the current City Council. "What a lot of people don't realize still is that the developer rights were granted over 20 years ago," Martin said. "Where the developers do have those rights that were granted and those entitlements, we can't make that change." Martin pointed to Rosser Lakes Preserve as an example of an area where the city was able to prevent additional development. She said a developer wanted to build 86 homes on the property, but the city instead acquired the land to preserve it as green space. Lucie has acquired more than 280 acres of green space since January 2025. Strazzeri said he supports what he calls responsible growth but believes infrastructure should be in place before communities are developed. "Our roads, our schools, our utilities, our emergency services need to be in place prior to them developing in these communities because they're playing catch up right now," Strazzeri said. Traffic All three candidates acknowledged traffic as a major issue, but offered different approaches. Giordano called traffic in St. Lucie West a "nightmare" and said he wants a new traffic study examining roadways, traffic signals and signal timing. "It takes almost 30 minutes to get from one end to the other," Giordano said of St. "That's totally unacceptable." He said the city should examine where roads could be widened, whether medians need to be removed and where other changes could improve traffic flow. Martin pointed to projects already underway, including work on Floresta Drive and Port St. Lucie Boulevard South, roundabouts in Torino and planned intersection improvements at Tradition Parkway and Village Parkway, Savona Boulevard and Gatlin Boulevard. She said roundabouts can help move vehicles more efficiently and the city is extending turn lanes where possible. "We're going to continue to look at all of our areas and do those intersection improvements so that we can keep the flow of traffic going to reduce that traffic congestion," Martin said. Strazzeri said the city needs to be "proactive and not reactive," calling for better traffic signal coordination, adaptive signal technology and road expansion where possible. "We have to ensure that the infrastructure keeps pace with the development," Strazzeri said. Who should pay for growth? The candidates also addressed concerns over whether developers are paying enough toward the infrastructure needed to support new development. Giordano said developers should be held accountable for infrastructure needs associated with their projects. "They need to pay their fair share if they're going to be coming here and developing," Giordano said, adding that if a project requires sidewalks or lights, developers should be responsible for those needs. Martin pushed back on the idea that developers are not already paying toward infrastructure. "All the developers are required to pay mobility or impact fees for roads, for parks, for law enforcement and for civic space," Martin said. She said the city periodically reviews and increases those fees, but noted state law limits how much municipalities can levy through impact and mobility fees. Strazzeri said he also believes developers should carry more of the burden associated with growth. "The developers have to pay their fair share," Strazzeri said. "This should not be pushed off to the residents." He said roads, schools, emergency services and utilities should be addressed as part of the development process. Property taxes, CDDs and housing costs Martin also addressed a distinction she said residents should understand when looking at what they pay to live in Port St. She said the city does not control housing prices or interest rates, but does control its own property tax rate. Lucie has lowered its property tax rate each year for the past 11 years, reducing the rate by 25% over that period. She also said 22% of a resident's property tax bill goes to the city, with the remainder going to other taxing authorities. Martin also addressed Community Development District assessments, or CDDs, which are common in parts of Tradition. She said those assessments are determined by their respective CDD boards, not the Port St. On housing affordability, Giordano said higher-paying jobs are an important part of making it possible for residents to afford homes. "We need to bring the jobs," Giordano said. Strazzeri acknowledged the city does not control the housing market or interest rates but said it can work on affordable housing and ensuring housing options exist for everyday workers. "Everybody deserves the right to afford a home," Strazzeri said. Giordano also tied housing affordability to the need for higher-paying jobs. He said he wants to attract investors, medical centers and technology companies to Port St. We need those $100,000 jobs for our community, Giordano said. Why do we have to travel to West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale or Miami? Strazzeri also said attracting higher-paying jobs could help residents afford to stay in the city. He said he would like to see Port St. Lucie become a technology hub rather than having residents leave for higher-paying work elsewhere. Trash collection Trash service is another issue that has generated debate in Port St. The city currently provides garbage collection once a week. Lucie voters will also get a chance to weigh in on trash service in the November general election, when a nonbinding question will ask whether residents support twice-weekly garbage pickup. Giordano said he supports allowing residents to decide service frequency and proposed creating a city-run trash operation instead of outsourcing collection. He estimated the city currently spends roughly $61 million outsourcing trash service and said he believes a city operation could provide the service for around $55 million while creating jobs. Those cost estimates are Giordano's and were not independently verified by CBS12 News. Strazzeri said he remains frustrated with trash service and also believes voters should have a say in how often their trash is collected. "We're paying more for less service, whereas previously we were paying less and getting more service," Strazzeri said. He said he has heard from residents who want twice-a-week pickup and others who prefer different service levels. The city has previously said twice-weekly collection would require more equipment and workers and would cost residents approximately $130 more per household each year. Soccer stadium and a downtown for Port St. Lucie One of the clearest differences between the candidates involves the planned minor league soccer stadium and the broader effort to create a downtown-like destination. Martin supports the project and said the stadium is intended to serve as an anchor for redevelopment on the city's east side. She said the city is not paying for the stadium itself, its operations or maintenance, or debt associated with it. "It's supposed to be the anchor to start attracting all those different uses of the retail, the shopping, the hotels to really redevelop that entire area so that we can have that walkable downtown-like destination point," Martin said. Giordano opposes the stadium and said he would try to stop it if possible. "If I can stop the soccer stadium, I will stop it," Giordano said. However, he said that if the project cannot be stopped, he would work to make the venue as profitable as possible by using it for concerts, graduations and other community events. Giordano said he does support creating a downtown and floated attracting investors and even a Seminole Hard Rock casino as possibilities. Strazzeri said he is not opposed to a downtown but does not believe it or the soccer stadium should be the city's priority right now. "I would really like to improve the roads," Strazzeri said. "I would like to bring, you know, Trader Joe's, a Topgolf, higher-paying jobs." He said Port St. Lucie should first focus on quality of life and other needs. "I'm not saying that I'm against a downtown, but right now we need to focus on other things," Strazzeri said. Water quality Water quality also came up during the candidate interviews. Giordano said he wants the city to stop chemical spraying in lakes and waterways, pointing to a fish kill at Sawgrass Lakes as an example of his concern. He attributed the deaths to spraying and said the practice would stop if he becomes mayor. Strazzeri similarly said he would prefer natural approaches, including aeration or dredging, over what he described as harsh chemicals. "I would prefer to find natural ways to fix these issues rather than using these harsh chemicals and killing the fish," Strazzeri said. Martin pointed to the city's existing water-quality programs, including the McCarty Ranch Water Quality Project, stormwater baffle boxes and other projects aimed at reducing nutrients and pollution. "We constantly have projects going that are all about water quality," Martin said. What would they prioritize in office? Martin said her top priority if reelected would continue to be public safety, followed by infrastructure, reducing traffic congestion and maintaining quality of life. She also pointed to what she considers accomplishments during her time in office, including lowering the city's millage rate, reducing city debt by more than $400 million and adding parks. Giordano said that during his first 100 days, he would focus on Flock license plate readers and red-light cameras as well as traffic patterns and signal timing. He said he would seek new traffic data to determine where the city can reduce congestion. Strazzeri said his first year would focus on increasing transparency between City Hall and residents. He proposed creating a small-business owner committee and holding quarterly town halls where residents could hear about upcoming city plans and provide feedback before decisions are made. He said he would also focus on higher-paying jobs and additional entertainment and dining options. Martin has served as Port St. Lucie's mayor for the past five years and previously served on the City Council. She was first elected in 2010 and said she has lived in Port St. Before elected office, Martin worked as a paralegal. Giordano said he has lived in Port St. Lucie since 1989, grew up and attended school in the city and has nearly 20 years of public-service experience. He said he spent about a decade with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, later worked in security at the nuclear power plant and is a local business owner. Strazzeri said he moved to Port St. He served in the Army, deployed to Iraq as a combat engineer and later transitioned into information technology and cybersecurity. He said he decided to run after his son died from cancer and his experiences led him to believe residents needed a stronger voice in local government. Why should voters choose them? Martin points to her experience. "I have the knowledge, experience, and the results-driven leadership in order to continue to make that happen, to continue to make Port St. Lucie the best it possibly can be," Martin said. Giordano describes himself as an alternative to longtime political leadership. I'm a local business owner," Giordano said. "I want to bring a different style of leadership that works for the community." Strazzeri said his campaign is centered on transparency and accountability. Lucie deserves leadership that's transparent, accountable, and independent and is only responsible to the people and not special interests," Strazzeri said. Lucie voters will make that decision Tuesday. Election Day information The Port St. Lucie mayoral race is nonpartisan, meaning candidates do not run with a political party affiliation. Polls close Tuesday at 7 p.m. If one candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, that candidate wins the mayoral race outright. If no candidate receives more than 50%, the top two vote-getters will advance to the November general election. CBS12 News will be tracking the Port St. Lucie mayoral race and election results throughout the night.

A small plane crashed into the water at South Beach Park in Boca Raton Saturday morning, and the wreckage was temporarily moved to nearby Silver Palm Park off Palmetto Park Road.The sole occupant of the plane, a female pilot, is expected to fully recover. She was taken to a hospital as a precaution following the crash.Witnesses at the scene said they saw the plane flying very low before it landed in the water.The Boca Raton Police Department was on scene at Silver Palm Park but could not independently confirm the wreckage is the same plane from Saturday's crash. However, the tail number visible on the plane matches the tail number in photos sent to our newsroom showing a plane in the water Saturday morning.At 8:30 a.m. Sunday, Fronte Crane Service out of Fort Lauderdale began removing the wreckage from the Silver Palm Park boat ramp. The Federal Aviation Administration is leading the investigation into the crash.What caused the plane to go down remains under investigation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A small-engine plane crash-landed in the water off Boca Raton Saturday, drawing stunned reactions from beachgoers and boaters who watched the scene unfold near South Beach Park at 250 South Ocean Blvd.Boca Raton Fire Rescue said only one woman was aboard the aircraft. She was able to exit the plane on her own. Lifeguards brought her to shore, where she was taken to the hospital as a precaution. No injuries were reported.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Brett Goorland, a tourist who had been snorkeling at nearby Red Reef Park, said he had a close-up view of the plane's final moments in the air."We looked down there was a school of snook, looked up, a plane came over us about 10 feet over us," Goorland said. "Bizarre site for sure."Michael Arizzi and his wife were on a boat nearby when they noticed something was wrong. Arizzi said he works in aviation and has experience with aircraft maintenance."The plane got lower in front of Palmetto. I'm like wow that's really risky, before I noticed the plane go into a glide path," Arizzi said. "At first you go, oh it's not an emergency, it's not an emergency, and then all of a sudden the plane hits the water."Arizzi credited the pilot for the safe outcome."That's kind of a flawless move for a pilot, is 'hey let me land in the water off the beach where there's lifeguards to help,' so that was an excellent move on the pilot and doing so in which it didn't put the public at risk," Arizzi said.The plane remained in the water Saturday and is expected to stay until it is retrieved Sunday.It is still unclear why the plane was forced to make an emergency landing on the water. Boca Raton Police said the FAA has taken over the investigation. The Coast Guard and Boca Raton Police are watching over the aircraft until it is removed.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Congressman Brian Mast is pointing to progress on some of the Treasure Coast’s biggest issues as he campaigns for a sixth term, while laying out what he says still needs to be done on taxes, transportation, water quality, and health concerns. In a wide-ranging one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, the Republican congressman discussed everything from Lake Okeechobee and Brightline to Florida’s rapid growth and concerns about a possible cancer cluster in St. The interview is part of CBS12 News’ continuing coverage of the race for Florida’s 21st Congressional District . CBS12 News had hoped to bring voters a debate between the Republican and Democratic nominees, but the Democratic primary remained too close to call for days. It was not until Friday that the Associated Press declared James Martin the winner by a little more than 300 votes. CBS12 News will sit down one-on-one with Martin next Friday to give voters a chance to hear directly from Mast’s Democratic opponent ahead of the November election. See also: James Martin wins Democratic primary, will face Brian Mast in Florida’s 21st District Mast, who has represented the area since 2017, said one of the accomplishments he is most proud of is the progress made toward reducing harmful Lake Okeechobee discharges into the St. He pointed to changes in the way the Army Corps of Engineers manages Lake Okeechobee, the construction of the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir, and increased federal funding for Everglades restoration. Mast said federal funding for ecosystem restoration has grown from roughly $60 million to $65 million a year when he entered office to hundreds of millions of dollars annually. He said those projects have helped dramatically reduce the threat of damaging discharges into the Treasure Coast’s waterways. I hope they look at it and they say, you know what? In 2016, when Brian Mast came into office, or before he came into office, we couldn't go and sit on our dock in our backyard because there were toxic algal blooms all around St. Lucie, all across the Treasure Coast, Mast said. Brightline station on the Treasure Coast Mast also said he wants Treasure Coast residents to get more benefit from Brightline trains that currently travel through the region without stopping. Absolutely, Mast said when asked whether he would like to see a Brightline presence on the Treasure Coast. If they're going to be instead of just a pass through through our community, a place where people can get on and get off, that would be a benefit. But Mast questioned whether taxpayers should be expected to shoulder the full cost of a new station. He said Brightline has sought public funding for a station that could cost tens of millions of dollars and suggested a less expensive passenger platform should at least be considered. Mast also highlighted roughly $220 million in funding for replacement of the aging Florida East Coast Railway bridge over the St. The new bridge is expected to provide significantly more clearance for boats, reducing conflicts between rail and marine traffic. Renewed push for cancer cluster investigation Mast also told CBS12 News he has asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to take another look at concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. The aggressive form of brain cancer has raised concerns among some families who believe the number of cases in the area warrants additional investigation. Previous state and federal reviews did not determine that a cancer cluster existed. Mast said the emergence of additional cases deserves another examination. I have requested again that the CDC come in, Mast said. We're seeing more instances of this aggressive brain tumor. You need to come in and you need to take a look. Mast said he wants federal health officials to provide residents with detailed data explaining how the cases were evaluated and whether there is any connection between them. Supporting Amendment 3 Mast also gave his full support to Amendment 3, which would increase Florida’s homestead exemption and reduce property taxes for qualifying homeowners. For Mast, the issue comes down to allowing Floridians to keep more of their money. I fully support reducing the tax burden, Mast said. Every dollar that we spend in government, at any level of government, federal or local, it comes out of your pocket. Cities, counties, and some public safety agencies have warned the amendment could reduce the money available to provide local services. Mast acknowledged there could be an impact on local budgets but said governments should also examine their own spending and look for places to cut. There are absolutely places that our cities and our counties can cut, Mast said. Growth and data centers With Port St. Lucie County experiencing explosive population growth, Mast said federal infrastructure funding will be an important part of keeping up. As a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, Mast said his role allows him to advocate for federal dollars for roads, bridges, airports and other major projects in the district. He also weighed in on the growing debate over massive data centers needed to power artificial intelligence and other technology. Mast acknowledged the country needs data centers but said that does not mean they need to be built in South Florida. Do they need to be in your backyard or in the 21st congressional district? Absolutely not, Mast said. He said those decisions ultimately belong to local communities, which have to weigh potential jobs and tax revenue against demands on electricity, water and the character of the community. Health care and affordability On health care, Mast said he does not support bringing back enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that were tied to the COVID-19 pandemic. Instead, he pointed to efforts to reduce prescription drug prices and said consumers should have more flexibility to choose health plans based on what they actually need. Mast also argued that reducing taxes is one of the most effective ways Washington can address affordability, pointing to tax reductions involving tips, overtime and Social Security. Iran and gas prices As chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Mast also defended the U.S. Mast argued Iran has targeted American interests and service members for years and said preventing the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon is critical to U.S. He acknowledged that instability in the Middle East has contributed to higher gas prices and said he supports eliminating the federal gasoline and diesel taxes as another way to lower prices at the pump. Term limits Despite seeking a sixth term himself, Mast said he supports congressional term limits and has signed a pledge committing to vote for them if legislation reaches the House floor. If he were writing the proposal, Mast said he would limit House members to three terms, or six years, while allowing one or possibly two Senate terms. Mast said his own record is what he wants voters to consider as he asks them for another term particularly his work on the Treasure Coast’s waterways, veterans, and taxes. I hope they say, you know what, Brian does what he says, Mast said.

A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel, ending a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in Indian River County. Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures, according to the sheriff’s office. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide. Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. “She had actually told her co-workers, ‘If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him, I’m not here,’” Flowers said. “She had broken things off with him, he had moved away and somehow she knew that he could potentially be coming to the area.” According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from an unknown location to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic’s Vero Beach home Sunday morning. “You see that video of him walking, he was dropped off around the corner, he made his way in, we’ve got him on video, on Ring doorbells, on a variety of different security cameras,” Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators. The sheriff’s office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle’s movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle’s ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. “At this moment, we don’t have charges on her, but we are actively speaking with her,” Flowers said. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle’s ex-wife, according to the sheriff’s office. Flowers credited the department’s license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. “I’m not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia,” Flowers said. “So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this.” The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic’s body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night — a timeline Flowers called “unbelievable police work.” Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday’s announcement. Waggle will be extradited back to Indian River County to face the first-degree murder charge. Crews are still working to pull a multi-million dollar, six-axle crane out of a ditch along 90th Avenue near Oslo Road in Vero Beach, after it went off the road and flipped on August 19th. She said she has driven it for 11 years. Rogers said this is not the first crash she has seen on this stretch of road, which she describes as narrow. She said crews closed 82nd Avenue and rerouted traffic for the Oslo Road project , and drivers looking for a fast route to State Road 60 and I-95 found this road instead. "The dump trucks and the semi trucks have learned that this is a thruway to 60 to get on 95," Rogers said. "It's quick, it's easy, it's a straight shot." Rogers said there is no signage warning drivers the road narrows, and she said dump trucks are not supposed to be using this route at all under the project's haul route plan. She said trucks were assigned to 82nd Avenue, and only started coming this way once that road closed. Rogers also raised concerns about a bridge at 4th Street, saying she has not seen a posted weight limit and doesn't know whether it can structurally handle the heavier commercial traffic now crossing it. She described another hazard when it rains. Water pools on the low side of the road and has nowhere to drain, she said, which hides what's underneath. "You don't know if there's a hole. You don't know if there's a soft spot. You don't know if there's a washout happening," Rogers said. Rogers said the traffic has made her change her own driving habits. When she sees a truck or semi approaching on the narrower sections, she said she pulls over and waits. "I stopped on the bridge, pulled off on the side there at 4th Street and waited for the semi to come and pass, because I know it's not wide enough to comfortably pass," Rogers said. "I'd rather not." She recounted a close call involving her husband, who was driving his Dodge 3500 dually when he passed another truck pulling a trailer on the road. "The trailers actually touched," Rogers said. Crews remain on scene working to remove the crashed crane. CBS12 News is asking the county if they plan on adding signage or directing trucks to go a different route. FDOT confirmed that this stretch of 90th Ave. is maintained by Indian River County. between 4th Street and Oslo Road will be closed until the truck is removed.

Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found “lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass.” The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal. Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions. “As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal’s personality come out,” Perea said. “When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down.” Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country. “Within two weeks, you wouldn’t even recognize that animal,” Perea said. “They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they’re meant to be.” Perea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under the law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said communities should watch for several warning signs that animal hoarding may be occurring nearby. “The smell will probably be your first indicator,” Perea said. “If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that’s also a big indicator.” Perea said the situation can escalate when people feel compassion for animals but lack the resources to properly care for them. “It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don’t have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that’s acceptable,” Perea said. The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued border collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation. The shelter is also asking for donations to its emergency medical fund or through its Amazon Wish List. Florida voters now have another way to crunch the numbers on Amendment 3, though the math still comes with plenty of political variables.Florida TaxWatch, the nonpartisan watchdog behind Florida’s annual “Budget Turkey” list, launched a new online resource center Friday designed to explain the sweeping property-tax proposal before the November election.Watch report from Forrest Saunders“With Amendment 3 on the November ballot, there is much discussion and confusion related to this proposed property-tax measure,” Florida TaxWatch Chair David Casey said.The Florida Property Tax Resource Center includes an interactive county map, local millage rates, frequently asked questions and estimates showing how much revenue local governments could lose if the amendment passes.Think less crystal ball, more fiscal X-ray.“This amendment would cut property tax locally by an estimated $45.8 billion over five years,” Florida TaxWatch President and CEO Jeff Kottkamp said.What Amendment 3 would changeAmendment 3 would expand Florida’s homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School property taxes would remain unchanged.The proposal would also reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. That category includes rental homes, second homes and commercial properties.The measure must receive at least 60% support from voters to become part of the Florida Constitution.TaxWatch has not yet taken an official position on the amendment. Kottkamp said the organization will announce its recommendation in a broader constitutional amendment guide expected next month.No personalized estimateOne feature missing from the new resource center is a calculator showing how much an individual homeowner could save.TaxWatch said such a figure would be too speculative because cities and counties could respond to the revenue loss by cutting services, increasing millage rates or imposing new fees and special assessments.However, a private calculator we previously featured allows homeowners to enter their taxable value and local millage rates to generate an estimate.The tool was created by Casey Vockell of My Exemption Check.“The impact to the local taxing authorities is going to be bad, but the benefit to the taxpayer is not going to be nearly as big as one might think,” Vockell said.In one example, the calculator found that a Hillsborough County home assessed at $500,000 could save less than $209 per month by 2028.The estimate does not account for any later decisions by local governments that could reduce or offset those savings.Opponents warn of service cutsThe amendment’s critics argue the proposal would shift costs rather than eliminate them, potentially forcing communities to reduce spending on police, firefighters, emergency medical services, libraries and other local programs.“The language on voters’ ballots may have changed, but that doesn’t change the fact that Amendment 3 is still a scam and a tax shift,” said Jackson Peel with Save Our Services. “That’s either going to raise our costs or take away services that Floridians rely on every day.”The ballot summary was recently rewritten after a Leon County judge found the Legislature’s original wording biased and misleading. The ruling did not remove the amendment from the ballot.DeSantis promises help for rural countiesSupporters, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, argue local governments can absorb the reductions by trimming spending. DeSantis has also promised state assistance for rural and fiscally constrained counties.If the amendment passes, DeSantis said lawmakers would need to return to Tallahassee for a special session to implement it. That would leave a short window before he leaves office in January.“I’d hate for people to deprive themselves of a really significant tax break because you think somehow they’re not going to have money to have a police force or something,” DeSantis said.Despite the governor’s backing, passage is not guaranteed. Amendment 3 must clear Florida’s 60% constitutional threshold in November.For voters, the new TaxWatch center supplies more numbers. The central question remains the same: How much stays in homeowners’ wallets, and what might disappear from their communities?

The city also used the firm S. Renee Narlock Associates, of Tallahassee, to hire Police Chief David Smith. Jasmaine McKinney arrived, she spoke directly to the gold vendor and worked with victim and the business to stop the transaction. The vendor cooperated with law enforcement, canceled the transaction and helped ensure the victim’s money was returned, according to the posting. Chairman Deryl Loar VERO BEACH – The Indian River County Commission voted unanimously Aug. 4 to approve a landmark Attainable Housing Trust that will operate under the guidelines of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership program and will encourage the use of surplus county-owned lands to more effectively support attainable housing developments in the county. Previously on May 27, the members of the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee voted unanimously to recommend the County Commission approve the draft ordinance. County SHIP Administrator Siphi Chinyanganya provided a comprehensive review of the proposal that morning. “We’re going to explain what the Attainable Housing Trust is and we’re hoping the ordinance will be approved today,” she said. “It supports affordable and attainable housing development. The ordinance establishes the Trust focused on land acquisition, land banking and partnerships with for-profit and non-profit organizations. We’re going to look at the legal framework, the ordinance overview and the implementation process of the Trust.” Chinyanganya first pointed out the distinction between the Attainable Housing Trust and the traditional SHIP program that provides local governments funding for affordable housing. “This is a separate fund from the SHIP local housing assistance program, but it aligns with SHIP-based practices,” she explained. “It will be administered by the SHIP administrator but will maintain independent accounting and compliance. So, while the SHIP program operates under the local housing assistance plan, the trust fund would maintain separate accounting compliance and reporting requirements. The purpose of this fund is to have affordable housing recognized as a public purpose authorized under Section 125-379 of Florida Statutes, which encourages counties to identify and use surplus county-owned lands for affordable housing.” The SHIP administrator plans to seek Attainable Housing Trust funding from voluntary developer contributions, proceeds from the sale or disposition of county-owned property, grants, donations and interlocal contributions, private philanthropy donations and even interest earnings on the trust fund balance itself. She emphasized the formal county hierarchy that will oversee all facets of attainable housing development under the AHT. “At the top of the Trust will be the Board of County Commissioners [with] final authority,” she continued. “The Community Services Department will administrate the program and coordinate any events. The Affordable Housing Advisory Committee will provide an advisory role; Planning Development will review and assess properties to be acquired; and finance, county administration and the county attorney will have oversight. The SHIP administrator will develop and publish a request for qualifications to create a register of development partners. The AHAC will review the RFQ and make recommendations for eligible development partners to the BOCC, and then the BOCC will approve the eligible development partners added to the register.” As far as the disposition of properties, the Planning Development Department will first evaluate the location, zoning and infrastructural viability of each property to assess developmental feasibility. The county attorney’s office will then verify the title status and draft acquisition and conveyance language, as well as securing BOCC authorization to purchase or accept the property. Planning Development staff will subsequently classify the property as surplus and designate it for attainable housing. The SHIP administrator and Community Services staff will in turn present available properties to the AHAC. The AHAC will offer available properties to partners on the register in order of ranking. Procurement and the SHIP administrator will coordinate the property conveyance following BOCC approval. The Trust has been in safeguards for the county as well. “There will be recorded affordability covenants, income limits and compliance requirements and long-term affordability protections,” Chinyanganya explained. “This will be a 50-year lean so that it remains affordable [and] developers will be responsible for ongoing compliance following conveyance. It limits county exposure to land transactions and ensures legal and financial safeguards. We also have financial controls through a special revenue fund.” Chairman Deryl Loar offered his perspective at the conclusion of her presentation, which brought a few chuckles from the dais. “This is actually another tool for our toolbox,” he said. “It is a trust that allows us – like other counties and municipalities – to have a mechanism in place. For example, if Commissioner [Joseph] Earman, donates $100,000 for affordable housing when he retires, we will certainly accept it, put it in trust and it will be policed as we do the current SHIP program.” When no members of the public came forward to comment afterward, District 2 Commissioner Joseph Flescher made a motion for approval. “Commissioner Earman just said that I was retiring beforehand, so I want to set up my commitment as well and we’ll take a look at that,” he said as laughter again broke out in the Chambers. “Motion to approve.” Commissioner Earman seconded that motion, which then passed unanimously. Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, a Vero Beach hairdresser, was killed outside her home on Aug. 16 by Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, of Sebastian, who then fled the area and was subsequently arrested in West Virginia. Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, a Vero Beach hairdresser, told fellow co-workers at a salon where she worked that she did not want anything to do with Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, of Sebastian, who later allegedly shot her outside her Vero Beach home on Aug. 16, Sheriff Eric Flowers said. The gun that Indian River County Sheriff’s Office found near the scene of the homicide of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, belonged to the ex-wife of Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, now charged with first-degree murder in Kriskewicz’s death. Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, was taken into custody on Aug. 19, at a motel in Dunbar, West Virginia by U.S. Marshals deputies for Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, which has charged Waggle with first-degree murder. Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, is facing a first-degree murder charge in the fatal shooting on Aug. 16 of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, outside her Vero Beach home in the 500 block of 1st Street, Vero Beach. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY – Indian River County Sheriff’s Office is now working to bring a murder suspect, arrested on Aug. 19 in West Virginia, to face a first-degree murder charge in Indian River County in the homicide death of a Vero Beach hairdresser, Sheriff Eric Flowers said at a press conference on Aug. Marshals deputies arrested Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, of Sebastian at a motel in Dunbar, West Virginia, about six miles west of Charleston, on Aug. Waggle was being sought by the sheriff’s office as a “person of interest” in the homicide of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, outside her home in the in the 500 block of 1st Street, Vero Beach. 16, detectives responded to a 911 call about a woman lying in the roadway at that address. Deputies located Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures. She was transported to a local trauma center, where she was later pronounced deceased. Waggle, who apparently was traveling alone, is suspected of traveling by a Greyhound bus from an unknown location to Orlando where he then rode in an Uber to a location near Kriskewicz’s home in Vero Beach, Flowers said. Waggle was in Vero Beach for no more than 15 minutes, during which “he murdered her in cold blood in the street,” Flowers said. He had specifically traveled to Vero Beach with the full intention of killing Kriskewicz, Flowers noted. Waggle and Kriskewic interacted during that 15 minutes but it is not known what was said, Flowers said. Kriskewic was concerned about Waggle, with whom she had a relationship with at one time, to the point of telling co-workers “if he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I’m not here,” Flowers said. Waggle left the gun behind, ordered another Uber to take him to Orlando, where he then rode another Greyhound bus to North Carolina and then made his way to a motel in West Virginia, Flowers said. Detectives are still working to piece together specifics about Waggle’s travel patterns before and after the murder, Flowers said. Detectives recovered the gun they believe was used to kill Kriskewicz. In tracing the gun, they found it was registered to Waggle’s ex-wife in West Virginia. She was taken into custody and led detectives to Waggle at the motel, Flowers said. It is not clear whether any charges will be filed against the ex-wife. “Our team has worked relatively non-stop for the last couple of days,” Flowers said. In addition, the agency’s Real Time Crime Center and the Flock network of license plate readers helped detectives track Waggle to the motel, Flowers said. Flowers also praised the partnership the agency has with the Marshals office and witnesses who contributed information which led to Waggle’s arrest. The case is still an active investigation, Flowers said. “There’s still so much more to do in this investigation. We have a case to build.” Your comment has been submitted. VERO BEACH – A 25-year-old Vero Beach man was arrested on July 17 on charges including attempted murder after a birthday party ended and no one would take him to a local bar, according to an arrest affidavit. Collin Ryan Smith, 25, of the 4900 block of Corsica Square in Vero Beach, was booked into the Indian River County Jail on July 17 at 3:49 a.m. Smith was in the Indian River County Jail as of July 21 on no bond for possession of a weapon/ammunition by a convicted felon, according to the jail web site. He also faces $150,000 bond for attempted murder; $50,000 bond for two counts of battery by strangulation; $25,000 bond for aggravated battery; $5,000 bond for criminal mischief; $5,000 bond each for DUI, driving while license suspended and refusal to submit to a DUI testing and possession of drug paraphernalia. At about 1:49 a.m., Indian River County sheriff’s deputies went to a home in the 2400 block of 86th Drive, Vero Beach on July 17 about a disturbance in progress. Four people told deputies that as a birthday party started to settle down, a man later identified as Smith wanted someone to take him to a local bar, according to the arrest affidavit. When no one offered, he started yelling and waking up people in the house, according to the arrest affidavit. One woman told Smith to leave but he grabbed her hair and dragged her down a hallway into a kitchen where he allegedly got on top of the woman and began choking her until she was unconscious, according to the arrest affidavit. Another woman told officers that when she came out of her room, Smith grabbed her by the hair, pulled her outside and threw her to the ground, according to the arrest affidavit. A third woman said she saw Smith throw a woman into a ditch outside the house and when she trip to stop him, he hit her in the mouth and threw her to the ground, according to the arrest affidavit. Smith then pressed her against the side of a car and pressed her neck, causing a restriction of blood flow to her head, according to the arrest affidavit. A man at the house saw Smith attacking the three women and he intervened by fighting Smith off them, according to the arrest affidavit. In a written statement, a neighbor said when he heard screaming, he went outside and saw a man pick a woman up and slam her to the ground before he started yelling at the man to stop hitting her. He said in the statement that he told one of the other women to call 911. Deputies found a bullet in one woman’s bedroom, which she said fell out of Smith’s pocket. Smith then left in a Ford Pickup truck. Deputies enacted a “be on the lookout” for nearby law enforcement units who were told to conduct a traffic stop if they saw the truck, according to the arrest affidavit. Smith was subsequently stopped in the 1400 block of 96 Street, Vero Beach. A glass smoking device was found in his pocket, according to the arrest affidavit. Smith, who officers said smelled of alcohol, denied he was drinking or hitting any of the women at the house. He also refused to take a breathalyzer test, according to the arrest affidavit. A man the Martin County Sheriff's Office referred to as a "brazen" robber is now facing felony charges, accused of a jewelry theft at the Treasure Coast Mall. It happened at Royal Jewelers, a kiosk inside the mall, on July 20. Security video from the mall shows a man standing at the counter of the kiosk. Chris Morales of the Martin County Sheriff’s Office identified the man as 25-year-old Dezmone Johnson. "He actually comes up and pretends to be a customer, engages with the clerk for a few minutes," Morales said. According to Morales, Johnson walked away at one point before returning to ask for a closer look at the jewelry. "The clerk brings out a tray of, let's say, seven or eight less expensive necklaces according to him, and he just grabs the tray and runs out," Morales said. The clerk at the store can be heard screaming as the suspect runs away with the necklaces. According to the police report, the necklaces are valued between $850 and $4,500 each, totaling more than $22,000 in stolen jewelry. Cameras outside the mall showed investigators the vehicle Johnson drove away in. "We were able to get the tag from that vehicle, making it pretty easy for us. The vehicle came back to an address in Lauderhill, so down in Broward County," Morales said. Detectives visited a pawn shop near the Lauderhill address and stopped in to ask if Johnson was a customer. "Lo and behold, the owner says, 'Yeah, he was just in here trying to pawn a few necklaces.' Again, making it pretty easy for our detectives," Morales said. Johnson was arrested shortly afterward. Morales expressed relief at the arrest, saying even though this specific robbery was not violent, the next one might have been. "I would say there's a great chance of that. He has a history of violence. He has access to weapons in his criminal history. I'm sure he's not afraid to use that in future endeavors," Morales said. Johnson is charged with robbery and grand theft. He spent a short time in the Broward County jail and is currently free on bond as he awaits trial. A judge has thrown out three code enforcement violations against Subculture Coffee, but the City of Delray Beach is still prohibiting the popular coffee shop from hosting its community events, according to a letter sent to the owner.A Palm Beach County Circuit Court judge reversed the city’s orders, ruling that Delray Beach failed to follow its own established rules for such enforcement actions.WATCH: Parking saga continuesThe owner, Rodney Mayo, says just after he paid a separate $10,000 overdue fee and celebrated the court’s decision, he was hand-delivered a letter from the assistant city attorney informing him the events were still not allowed.“Tuesday I thought we’re all back on and we’re all good,” Mayo told WPTV. “Then I get a hand-delivered letter that says just because you won the appeal, does not mean that you are allowed to do these events.”The Court’s RulingThe appeals court found that the city’s Special Magistrate rulings against Subculture Coffee lacked the required written findings of fact and conclusions of law.According to the court’s opinion, Delray Beach's own operating guidelines mandate these formal sections in all rulings. Lucie man faces multiple charges involving a minor after officers served a search warrant at a home Thursday morning, authorities said. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. at a residence in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. During the operation, officers arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz without incident Police said Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. The response drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Authorities said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry into the home. "It's a diversion to either make entry. When conducting a high-risk operation, these are utilized just for the safety of both the officers and the individual," police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation and say they are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active. "As a father of three myself, we take it very serious anytime there is a child involved," Martinez said. Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. TLC Engineering Solutions will assess the structural needs of the Means Court Building, 532 N. 13th St., at a cost not to exceed $24,900, then report the findings and estimated costs back to the city for future action. FORT PIERCE – A historic former school building donated to the City of Fort Pierce could cost local taxpayers an estimated $2 million to install a new heating/cooling system, replace the roof and repair exterior wall leaks. The Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency (FPRA) has retained TLC Engineering Solutions to assess the structural needs of the Means Court Building, 532 N. 13th St., at a cost not to exceed $24,900, then report the findings and estimated costs back to the city for future action. City Engineer Mark Zrallack told the FPRA board earlier this month that he had inspected the building several times and recommended that the outside engineering firm be retained to conduct a comprehensive structural inspection. Means Court is the site of a former all-black public school in Fort Pierce and is considered a historic site in the Lincoln Park neighborhood. It was donated to the city by St. Most recently, the building was leased to Incubate Neighborhood Center (INC), a non-profit organization created to be a business development, education and community services center in the low-income neighborhood. The city signed a $12-a-year lease with INC in October 2021, and the organization initially took over operations there using about $500,000 in public donations – the largest coming from Allegany Franciscan Ministries (AFM). However, the building has been closed to occupancy for the past several years due to building code violations. In December 2024, the FPRA approved an amendment to its lease with INC, “requiring additional clarification and/or shifting of responsibility) to address several major building deficiencies.” Recently city officials had estimated the costs of a new heating/cooling system, new roof and repairing leaking exterior walls and windows could reach $2 million. A Lake Worth woman is facing a $26,000 repair bill for her Lexus after she says she unknowingly pumped diesel fuel from a premium gasoline pump at a Mobil gas station in Westlake. The incident, which left her car's engine destroyed, may have affected multiple other drivers who are now sharing similar stories.WATCH: WPTV asks, who is responsible?Ellie Ferguson said she stopped at the Mobil station at the intersection of Persimmon Boulevard and Seminole Pratt Whitney Road to fill up her tank before driving home after a dinner with her grandchildren.Ferguson told WPTV's Western Palm Beach County reporter, Michael Hoffman she selected the premium 93-octane gasoline and pumped nearly 14 gallons. About 15 minutes into her drive, the situation turned dire."My car just started rattling and shaking and just engine shut down," Ferguson said.She had her Lexus towed to a dealership, where she learned the cause of the catastrophic failure."They called me the next day and said, 'We found diesel in your tank,'" Ferguson recounted. "And I said, 'There is no way I put diesel in my car. I put 93.'"Dealership mechanics informed her the damage was extensive, requiring a complete engine replacement at a cost of $26,000.A review of local social media groups suggests Ferguson is not the only driver affected. Multiple posts on a Westlake community Facebook page show other customers complaining of identical issues after buying premium gasoline from the same Mobil station around the same time.To understand the mechanical impact, Hoffman spoke with an automotive expert."It can be catastrophic for your engine, and you don't really know that you're pumping it into your car until it's too late," said Todd Bender, a manager at Angel's Autobody.Bender explained that, in a best-case scenario, a car will run poorly. "Worst case scenario, it'll actually lock up your motor and hydrolock it, and it can damage the internals of your engine and require it to be replaced," he said.Hoffman began pressing for answers about who is responsible for the costly damages.A spokesperson for ExxonMobil, which licenses the Mobil brand, stated, “We do not own or operate retail stations in Florida. The manager confirmed the station was aware of the problem and said steps were being taken to address it.The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, which regulates fuel pumps, has been contacted regarding the number of official complaints filed against the station. Hoffman is awaiting that data.Ferguson said the station's management called her and instructed her to file an insurance claim against them. However, her request for that instruction in writing has so far gone unanswered."It's not right," Ferguson said. "It's not right."WPTV will continue to press the station's owner for a response and investigate how diesel ended up in a gasoline pump, how many drivers were affected, and who will be held responsible for the damages.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Abandoned and derelict boats are filling up Wildcat Cove off North Hutchinson Island in Fort Pierce, creating safety hazards and environmental concerns for residents and visitors. Philipe Chibas, who lives nearby and runs Hot Reels Offshore Adventures, described the area as a "boat junkyard." "Looks like Water World out here," Chibas said. "I have to navigate through this minefield every time I go out with customers." Chibas also expressed concerns about the environmental impact of the abandoned vessels. The boats are located between two nature preserves. The issue follows the city’s implementation of a new ordinance limiting boats to anchoring in the water for 45 days before requiring them to be moved. However, Chibas said Wildcat Cove is outside the restricted zone, allowing the problem to persist. "Instead of solving the problem, they pushed the problem somewhere else," he said. The area is also a popular spot for tubing and jet skiing, and residents are calling for the boats to be removed before an accident occurs. "They should be towed and destroyed," Chibas said. "You can’t leave your car on 95." The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said it has issued several citations and is continuing to monitor the situation.
