School District of Indian River County Superintendent Dr. Moore announced Wednesday he will conclude his tenure with the district effective June 30, 2027, after nearly seven years of service. “I am proud of what we have accomplished, but even more so of what we have built together,” Moore said. “Serving as Superintendent of Schools has been one of the greatest privileges of my professional life. Nearly seven years later, my belief in the power of public education to transform lives is stronger than ever.” Moore said in a news release that he shared his decision with school board members and his Cabinet Leadership Team before informing district and school leaders and broader SDIRC staff. His tenure currently ranks as the second longest among Florida’s appointed district school superintendents. He said during his time leading the district, SDIRC advanced from 38th to 5th among Florida’s 67 school districts based on District Grade, earned 4 consecutive A district grades, and grew the share of schools earning an A or B from 47 percent to 100 percent. The district also achieved a 96 percent high school graduation rate and was named the No. 1 Best Place to Teach in Florida by Niche for 2026. Moore said was named the 2025 Florida Superintendent of the Year and a national finalist. “These accomplishments tell an extraordinary story of improvement, but they are not the story itself. They are the evidence of the story,” Moore said in the release. “The story is what happens when beliefs become behaviors, behaviors become habits, and habits become coherent systems of work.” As Moore enters his final school year, he identified two priorities: ensuring every SDIRC school earns an A grade and positioning the district to become the No. 1 school district in Florida. “We have spent close to seven years proving that dramatic improvement is possible,” he said. “This year, I want us to demonstrate just how far a mature, coherent, high-performing system can go.” Following his departure, Moore said he intends to explore opportunities to help other leaders and school systems create conditions for exceptional student outcomes. The man accused of grabbing an entire display of gold chains from a jewelry kiosk at Treasure Coast Square Mall and fleeing on foot has been arrested and has already bonded out of jail, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . According to the sheriff's office, the robbery happened July 20 at the Royal Jewelers kiosk near the mall's main entrance in Jensen Beach. Investigators say a man approached the counter and asked to see several gold chains, trying some on before handing them back and walking away. He briefly left the mall, then returned and told the employee his girlfriend thought the chains he'd looked at were too expensive, asking to see cheaper options. When the employee pulled out a new display holding 9 gold chains, deputies say the man suddenly grabbed the entire display out of her hands and ran. He fled through the same entrance he'd come in, past a Ruby Tuesday and Port Barna Restaurant, and got into a silver Ford Fusion that was later seen on nearby surveillance video heading south on Federal Highway. The sheriff's office says the stolen merchandise was worth more than $22,000. Three of the necklaces were later recovered, two of them found on the ground near the mall's south exit, leaving six chains valued at roughly $13,000 still missing. Investigators say a Sheriff's Office crime scene unit lifted fingerprints and palm prints from the glass display counter where the suspect had been handling the chains, along with DNA from necklaces he tried on and a pair of sunglasses that fell off while he was running. Deputies say those prints matched 25-year-old Dezmone Karlde' Rome Johnson of Lauderhill. The sheriff's office says Johnson already had an open felony warrant out for a probation violation at the time of the robbery. Investigators say he was also spotted the following day at a Broward County pawn shop with a woman who may have pawned one of the stolen chains. An arrest warrant was approved and filed in the Martin County case, and Johnson was taken into custody July 31 by the Broward County Sheriff's Office with the help of the U.S. Marshals Fugitive Task Force. He recently bonded out of the Broward County Jail on separate charges. Sheriff John Budensiek explains why the arrest came more than a week after the robbery. "The next day, we had fingerprints from our suspect. Immediately we had a tag from the car in a description, but we wanted to kind of put it all together and do it the right way, as opposed to hastily running out and making an arrest that could or could not be beat in a court," said Budensiek. See also: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The sheriff described Johnson as having an extensive criminal history, including prior arrests involving firearms charges and resisting. "He's been through the system, but he's used to the revolving door system," Budensiek said. "That's not going to be the case here. If you steal $22,000 worth of anything from one of our Martin County businesses or residences, the 19th Circuit will lock you up, and you're likely to do prison time here in our circuit." Budensiek said Johnson will face the Martin County charges in addition to the felony probation violation warrant out of Broward County, and said investigators don't yet know why Johnson specifically targeted the Treasure Coast Square Mall. He also cautioned that mall kiosks like Royal Jewelers can be especially vulnerable, since they typically have fewer security cameras and safeguards than storefront businesses, and said this year alone the mall has seen multiple snatch-and-grab incidents targeting kiosks. He encouraged vendors to ask for identification or proof of funds from customers requesting to see high-value merchandise.

A man accused of traveling to Indian River County with the intent to kill his ex-girlfriend, a Vero Beach hairdresser, was captured in West Virginia after a four-day investigation that authorities say was aided by license plate reader technology. We got a murderer behind bars because of this, Sheriff Eric Flowers said, referring to the license plate reader system. "We've got him on video on ring doorbells on a variety of different security cameras." The investigation began Sunday morning, when authorities found Dawn Kriskewic’s body in a roadway in the southern part of the county. Officials said investigators initially did not know who she was and had not previously encountered her. Investigators say Waggle traveled to Vero Beach by bus and Uber before allegedly killing Dawn Kriskewic outside her home Sunday morning. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said surveillance video captured Waggle walking through Kriskewic's neighborhood shortly after an Uber dropped him off. He was there for 10, 15 minutes tops," Flowers said. "He murdered her in cold blood in the street. Investigators say Waggle then left the area, taking an Uber back to Orlando before boarding another Greyhound bus. He eventually made his way to West Virginia, where investigators say he hid at a motel. By Wednesday night, authorities had tracked Waggle to a motel in West Virginia and taken him into custody. This has been an absolutely incredible case for them to put this together and make all of this happen in such a short amount of time, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a news conference. Authorities said Kriskewic had ended her relationship with Waggle before the shooting and had warned coworkers at the hair salon that she wanted no contact with him. She had actually told her coworkers at the hair salon, If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I’m not here,’ the sheriff said. Flowers believes the killing was motivated by domestic violence and control. It's all about power, control, domestic violence, he said. Investigators believe Waggle traveled to the area specifically to kill Kriskewic. Waggle came here to Indian River County fully intent on shooting and killing Dawn, the sheriff said. That was his entire premise. According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus to Orlando before taking an Uber to Indian River County. Surveillance footage, including Ring doorbell video and other security cameras, captured him walking toward Kriskewic’s residence after being dropped off nearby. Authorities said Waggle and Kriskewic had a brief interaction before he shot her and fled. He walked to the residence. They had a brief interaction. He shot her, and then he fled that area, the sheriff said. Investigators said Waggle then took an Uber back to Orlando, boarded another Greyhound bus and traveled to North Carolina before eventually making his way to West Virginia. Authorities said no one appeared to have traveled with him. Investigators interviewed the Uber drivers who transported Waggle and found that he had a single bus ticket. Sheriff credits network of license plate readers The sheriff credited the agency’s Real Time Crime Center and a network of license plate readers with helping investigators piece together Waggle’s movements and locate him. For everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this, the sheriff said. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system. The sheriff clarified that Flock is one brand of automated license plate reader used by law enforcement. We’ve made so many cases, and we’ve protected this community as a result of this, and this is just another example of that, he said. Investigators also focused on Waggle’s ex-wife, who was in West Virginia and had been communicating with him. Authorities said the Real Time Crime Center determined she had been making calls to a specific motel. Investigators eventually found Waggle at that same motel. The sheriff said the gun believed to have been used in the killing belonged to Waggle’s ex-wife and that she knew he had it. Two detectives were sent to West Virginia to interview both Waggle and his ex-wife and determine how much she knew about his plans and what assistance, if any, she provided. She was at the hotel, the same hotel that we got him at, the sheriff said. So they were definitely in communication. We don’t know what extent, what she knew. We don’t know if she knew his plans. See also: Former Vero Beach Eagles secretary accused of blowing nearly $419K on guns, liquor, LEGOs No charges had been announced against the ex-wife at the time of the news conference. Authorities said the investigation remains active as detectives continue working to establish Waggle’s movements before and after the shooting, including where his trip began, how he traveled from North Carolina to West Virginia and the circumstances surrounding his stay at the motel. The sheriff also praised witnesses who came forward during the investigation, saying their cooperation helped detectives build the case. Waggle is expected to be returned to Florida, although the timing could depend on whether he agrees to extradition or challenges the process. There’s still so much more to do in this investigation, the sheriff said. We’ve got a case to build.

A Lake Worth woman is facing a $26,000 repair bill for her Lexus after she says she unknowingly pumped diesel fuel from a premium gasoline pump at a Mobil gas station in Westlake. The incident, which left her car's engine destroyed, may have affected multiple other drivers who are now sharing similar stories.WATCH: WPTV asks, who is responsible?Ellie Ferguson said she stopped at the Mobil station at the intersection of Persimmon Boulevard and Seminole Pratt Whitney Road to fill up her tank before driving home after a dinner with her grandchildren.Ferguson told WPTV's Western Palm Beach County reporter, Michael Hoffman she selected the premium 93-octane gasoline and pumped nearly 14 gallons. About 15 minutes into her drive, the situation turned dire."My car just started rattling and shaking and just engine shut down," Ferguson said.She had her Lexus towed to a dealership, where she learned the cause of the catastrophic failure."They called me the next day and said, 'We found diesel in your tank,'" Ferguson recounted. "And I said, 'There is no way I put diesel in my car. I put 93.'"Dealership mechanics informed her the damage was extensive, requiring a complete engine replacement at a cost of $26,000.A review of local social media groups suggests Ferguson is not the only driver affected. Multiple posts on a Westlake community Facebook page show other customers complaining of identical issues after buying premium gasoline from the same Mobil station around the same time.To understand the mechanical impact, Hoffman spoke with an automotive expert."It can be catastrophic for your engine, and you don't really know that you're pumping it into your car until it's too late," said Todd Bender, a manager at Angel's Autobody.Bender explained that, in a best-case scenario, a car will run poorly. "Worst case scenario, it'll actually lock up your motor and hydrolock it, and it can damage the internals of your engine and require it to be replaced," he said.Hoffman began pressing for answers about who is responsible for the costly damages.A spokesperson for ExxonMobil, which licenses the Mobil brand, stated, “We do not own or operate retail stations in Florida. Recommend that you contact the owner/branded wholesaler for comment.”After multiple emails and calls to the corporation listed as the property owner went unanswered, Hoffman finally reached a manager at the Westlake station by phone. The manager confirmed the station was aware of the problem and said steps were being taken to address it.The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, which regulates fuel pumps, has been contacted regarding the number of official complaints filed against the station. Hoffman is awaiting that data.Ferguson said the station's management called her and instructed her to file an insurance claim against them. However, her request for that instruction in writing has so far gone unanswered."It's not right," Ferguson said. "It's not right."WPTV will continue to press the station's owner for a response and investigate how diesel ended up in a gasoline pump, how many drivers were affected, and who will be held responsible for the damages.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Crews are still working to pull a multi-million dollar, six-axle crane out of a ditch along 90th Avenue near Oslo Road in Vero Beach, after it went off the road and flipped on August 19th. For people who live nearby, the crash is the latest example of a problem they say they've been warning the county about for months. Sally Rogers lives down the road from where the crane came to rest. She said August 19th was when she first noticed the crane in the ditch. She drives this stretch of 90th Avenue constantly. "Every single day," Rogers said, when asked how often she travels the road. She said she has driven it for 11 years. Rogers said this is not the first crash she has seen on this stretch of road, which she describes as narrow. She said she does not know for certain what caused each past crash, but she believes the road itself is part of the problem. See also: 'Disgusting and shameful': Lantana mayor condemns vandalism at police memorial Rogers pointed to a recent detour as the reason commercial trucks are on this road at all. She said crews closed 82nd Avenue and rerouted traffic for the Oslo Road project , and drivers looking for a fast route to State Road 60 and I-95 found this road instead. "The dump trucks and the semi trucks have learned that this is a thruway to 60 to get on 95," Rogers said. "It's quick, it's easy, it's a straight shot." Rogers said there is no signage warning drivers the road narrows, and she said dump trucks are not supposed to be using this route at all under the project's haul route plan. She said trucks were assigned to 82nd Avenue, and only started coming this way once that road closed. Rogers also raised concerns about a bridge at 4th Street, saying she has not seen a posted weight limit and doesn't know whether it can structurally handle the heavier commercial traffic now crossing it. She described another hazard when it rains. Water pools on the low side of the road and has nowhere to drain, she said, which hides what's underneath. "You don't know if there's a hole. You don't know if there's a soft spot. You don't know if there's a washout happening," Rogers said. Rogers said the traffic has made her change her own driving habits. When she sees a truck or semi approaching on the narrower sections, she said she pulls over and waits. "I stopped on the bridge, pulled off on the side there at 4th Street and waited for the semi to come and pass, because I know it's not wide enough to comfortably pass," Rogers said. "I'd rather not." She recounted a close call involving her husband, who was driving his Dodge 3500 dually when he passed another truck pulling a trailer on the road. "The trailers actually touched," Rogers said. Rogers said she has asked Indian River County to conduct a traffic study on the road. She said the response so far has been noncommittal. "Maybe we'll do that, but I think right now we should wait," Rogers said the county told her. Her request now is simple: she wants county officials to come see the road for themselves. They need to lay eyes on it," Rogers said. Bring a county dump truck to go the opposite direction, and pass the county dump truck in the narrowest part of the road." Crews remain on scene working to remove the crashed crane. CBS12 News is asking the county if they plan on adding signage or directing trucks to go a different route. County officials say they're looking into the matter. FDOT confirmed that this stretch of 90th Ave. is maintained by Indian River County. between 4th Street and Oslo Road will be closed until the truck is removed.

Paige O'Donnell has legally surrendered the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed with WPTV on Friday, clearing the way for the dogs to be adopted.Staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations so adopters receive clear information about any long-term needs before placement decisions are made, the organization said. The dogs also will be prepared for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside animals already in the shelter’s care.Adoption applications will be available here and the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page beginning Sept. Applicants will be highly vetted to ensure appropriate matches, and applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups also will be available beginning Sept. 1.To keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services, the shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time.WATCH BELOW: Healing begins for animals rescued in Martin County hoarding casesO'Donnell faces 72 charges in what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case it has ever seen. The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month. A WPTV investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe into the case.Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."WATCH BELOW: Deputies describe 'the filth' involved in rescuing 36 neglected dogsThe Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal.Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."WATCH BELOW: 'Worst case we've ever seen': Humane Society caring for 36 rescued dogsPerea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under the law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said communities should watch for several warning signs that animal hoarding may be occurring nearby."The smell will probably be your first indicator," Perea said. "If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that's also a big indicator."Perea said the situation can escalate when people feel compassion for animals but lack the resources to properly care for them."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," Perea said.The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued Border Collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation. The shelter is also asking for donations to its emergency medical fund or through its Amazon Wish List.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel, ending a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in Indian River County. Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures, according to the sheriff’s office. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide. Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. “She had actually told her co-workers, ‘If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him, I’m not here,’” Flowers said. “She had broken things off with him, he had moved away and somehow she knew that he could potentially be coming to the area.” According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from an unknown location to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic’s Vero Beach home Sunday morning. “You see that video of him walking, he was dropped off around the corner, he made his way in, we’ve got him on video, on Ring doorbells, on a variety of different security cameras,” Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators. The sheriff’s office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle’s movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle’s ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. “At this moment, we don’t have charges on her, but we are actively speaking with her,” Flowers said. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle’s ex-wife, according to the sheriff’s office. Flowers credited the department’s license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. “I’m not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia,” Flowers said. “So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this.” The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic’s body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night — a timeline Flowers called “unbelievable police work.” Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday’s announcement. Waggle will be extradited back to Indian River County to face the first-degree murder charge. Paige O'Donnell has legally surrendered the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed with WPTV on Friday, clearing the way for the dogs to be adopted.Staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations so adopters receive clear information about any long-term needs before placement decisions are made, the organization said. The dogs also will be prepared for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside animals already in the shelter’s care.Adoption applications will be available here and the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page beginning Sept. Applicants will be highly vetted to ensure appropriate matches, and applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups also will be available beginning Sept. 1.To keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services, the shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time.WATCH BELOW: Deputies describe 'the filth' involved in rescuing 36 neglected dogsO'Donnell faces 72 charges in what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case it has ever seen. The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month. A WPTV investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe into the case.Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."WATCH BELOW: Healing begins for animals rescued in Martin County hoarding casesThe Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal.Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."WATCH BELOW: 'Worst case we've ever seen': Humane Society caring for 36 rescued dogsPerea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under the law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said communities should watch for several warning signs that animal hoarding may be occurring nearby."The smell will probably be your first indicator," Perea said. "If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that's also a big indicator."Perea said the situation can escalate when people feel compassion for animals but lack the resources to properly care for them."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," Perea said.The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued Border Collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation. The shelter is also asking for donations to its emergency medical fund or through its Amazon Wish List.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Miami woman accused of posing as a bank representative to scam a Martin County senior is now facing an additional charge after deputies say she tried to smuggle thousands of dollars in cash into jail hidden in an unexpected hiding spot her lady parts. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Monquie Love Turnbull never mentioned she was carrying $3,180 in cash concealed in her body when she was arrested, and the money wasn't discovered until she was being processed into the jail. The sheriff's office has since confirmed the cash is the same money taken from one of her alleged scam victims. Sheriff John Budensiek said Turnbull revealed she had the money inside her body when she complained of pain during a jail phone call to an unknown man. "Our detectives went back over to the jail. They interviewed her yet again. She admitted to having money inside of her. She said at that point it was only $400. And then later, as they interviewed her a little more, she said it was $3,180," said Budensiek. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office , the case began Monday when 31-year-old Monquie Love Turnbull showed up at an elderly victim's home claiming the person's bank account had been compromised. She told the victim she was with the bank and offered to take the debit or credit card off their hands to dispose of it safely. The victim grew suspicious of the encounter and contacted law enforcement, giving deputies time to track Turnbull down before she left the county. Arrest affidavits show the scheme was more coordinated than initially known. Investigators say an unidentified male caller, posing as a Chase Bank fraud representative, told the victim her account had been compromised and that someone would come to her home to collect and destroy her card before a replacement arrived. Turnbull, using the alias "Monica," then arrived at the home, verified herself with a code relayed from the caller, and collected the card, cutting it in half in front of the victim and placing the pieces in a manila envelope. The victim told deputies she grew uneasy and wrote down Turnbull's license plate number as she left. Minutes later, the victim's bank account was drained through a $3,000 withdrawal and a $180 ATM withdrawal, a total of $3,180. "In this particular instance, this was all the money that this lady had. This was everything that she had. And she handed it over to a scammer," said Budensiek. While deputies were investigating that report, the sheriff's office says they were alerted to a second call identifying Turnbull as a possible suspect in a nearly identical incident targeting another victim the same day. That attempt was caught on a Ring doorbell camera, but the second victim's family member grew skeptical and refused to hand over the card. That victim also provided a plate number and vehicle description, which helped investigators track Turnbull down. Deputies located the vehicle, a gray two-door Nissan Altima, on Bridge Road in Hobe Sound near the I-95 interchange and conducted a traffic stop. Body camera footage shows deputies pulling her over during the stop and placing her under arrest, with the arresting deputy telling her she was being taken into custody for a scheme to defraud. The first victim was brought to the scene and positively identified Turnbull as "Monica" from about 15 feet away. A search of the vehicle turned up a surgical mask and multiple yellow envelopes matching witness descriptions. Turnbull was booked on charges including scheme to defraud, grand theft, fraudulent use of a credit or debit card without consent involving a victim 60 or older, fraudulent use of ID without consent, and felony use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. Investigators say her cellphone and Apple Watch were seized, and a search warrant for the devices is pending. The Sheriff says there are still missing details in this investigation. She stated that she is part of a larger organization. We can't verify that one way or the other, and then the other question we have is: How does she know where to go? She went to two Chase Bank customers. Just random addresses, but it doesn't look to be that random," Budensiek said. See also: Suspended PBC clerk Mike Caruso makes first appearance on child sex abuse charges Turnbull now faces a charge of introducing contraband into a corrections facility on top of her original charges. She's being held on a $500,000 bond. The investigation remains open, including efforts to identify the second suspect who made the phone calls. The Martin County Sheriff's Office is renewing its warning to residents, especially seniors, not to let anyone into their home who wasn't scheduled to be there, and never to hand over cash, credit cards or valuables to someone who shows up unannounced. Anyone approached by someone claiming to represent a bank, financial institution or other organization asking for valuables or access to their home is urged not to comply and to call 911 instead.

This week I'm at Vero Beach High School where students are getting ready to go back to school, and I decided to do something I've never done before – I joined the marching band! I crashed band camp at Vero Beach High School just a few days before school started, and let me tell you, it was an incredible experience.WATCH: The first time I stepped onto that practice field, I could feel the history before I even picked up my instrument. This wasn't just another high school band – this was a tradition stretching back to 1934, when the Fighting Indians Band was founded as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Every student who had ever worn that uniform had helped build an incredible legacy.I got to meet some amazing students who are keeping that tradition alive, like Annabel Robbins who plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader."It's kind of scary, you know," Brady said. "You're in charge of a lot of kids, so you got to make sure they're all doing good.The band director, Sean Srigley, has a special connection to this program that goes way back. "I'm actually alumni of Vero Beach High School. I was in the band myself," Srigley explained. "The cool thing about Vero is we've got awesome academics, awesome athletics. Our band is right there with them. We've marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America."And he's not exaggerating! This band has an absolutely incredible resume. They performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing "Alexander's Ragtime Band" for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members.But that's not all – they've also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall! The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing our Treasure Coast with pride.After learning about all this amazing history, it was time for me to get to work. But honestly, that wasn't really my thing, so I tried the drums next.But joining the marching band for practice meant more than just learning music and drill. It meant discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in that Florida heat – something these kids do with incredible dedication.As I marched onto the football field, I couldn't help but imagine all the students who had stood in that same place before me. Some had gone on to march through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Others had performed in famous bowl games or international parades.As I left Vero Beach High School that day, I was thankful for the opportunity to be part of something so special, even for just one practice. These students aren't just making music – they're carrying on a legacy that's been building for nearly 90 years.

Staff at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast (HSTC) in Palm City are in the midst of an arduous process: medically grooming, bathing and examining 36 Border Collies brought to them Monday by Martin County deputies. Their fur was caked with feces and mats the size of apples."This is the worst case we've ever seen," said Sarah Fisher, a spokeswoman for HSTC. "We've seen throughout the years a dog or a cat, here and there, coming in with severe medical needs, but not 36 of them in this shape all at the same time."WATCH BELOW: 'Worst case we've ever seen': Humane Society caring for 36 rescued dogsDeputies rescued the Border Collies from a Palm City home Monday. Videos released by the sheriff's office show feces piled inches high inside the home and dogs that were so filthy that they blended in with the garbage and feces around them."Right now they're very, very shut down. Some of them aren't even walking. They're just laying on their sides," Fisher said. "We're going one by one and we are shaving-- cutting down the mats, and trying to see the extent of their medical (needs)."Fisher said many of the dogs have eye and skin infections, requiring special care during a shaving process that can take an hour for each dog."As we're cutting and we're shaving, we're finding lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass," Fisher said. "We did shave a puppy and three pounds of mats came off her."The dogs' former owner, Paige O'Donnell, was arrested Monday as deputies broke through her door. According to her arrest affidavit, she was taking a bath when law enforcement arrived to serve a warrant.O'Donnell now faces 72 criminal charges: one felony animal torture charge and one misdemeanor confinement charge for each dog. She remains in the Martin County Jail with bond set at $270,000.The 11-page affidavit details a renewed interest from investigators in O'Donnell's home after WPTV shared a neighbor's complaint with the sheriff's office. That neighbor, and others, had been reporting concerns about a large number of dogs at O'Donnell's home since at least 2020. A WPTV investigation that aired last week, before O'Donnell's arrest, detailed previous attempts by the sheriff's office to investigate, as O'Donnell continued to wall herself off from law enforcement.As deputies kept an eye on O'Donnell's home and began to ask her questions in July, the affidavit describes deceptive behavior from O'Donnell. She would not let deputies into her home, and blaming the stench that lingered across the road on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."After multiple canceled meetings with investigators, O'Donnell eventually agreed to meet in a park with one dog, which she said was one of only four she owned, according to the affidavit."It was... evident that he had been freshly bathed, as his coat was still wet," animal control officer Tabitha Queen wrote of the meeting. "I observed that Paige had attempted to cut away some of the matted fur; however, his coat remained matted and unkempt."Asked why the dog's fur was stained, "she stated she did not see anything."When deputies arrived at O'Donnell's home Monday, she was asked about the conditions of the home and dogs. "She only said she was in the process of cleaning it," the affidavit said."My heart's completely broken," Fisher said. "It hurts so bad knowing that these animals trusted a human. They trust humans and that these humans do this to them."Donna Turner and Tina Smith visited the Humane Society Tuesday after seeing images of Monday's rescue."We were just heartbroken," Smith said."Neighbors have pitched in towels and blankets and everything else, so we're just trying to help out," Turner said, as she and Smith hauled bags of dog food and clean towels from their car to the lobby. "We're just trying to help out."The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is asking for the public's help, particularly after also taking in more than 100 animals from another alleged hoarder in July."Our biggest need is monetary donations to our emergency medical fund," Fisher said. "This is depleting our emergency medical fund."Fisher said the Border Collies will not be ready to leave the Humane Society any time soon, but there are adoptable animals available now. They're running a name-your-own-price promotion to encourage adoptions and clear space in the shelter.Click here to see adoptable animals or make a donation.

According to Florida's Insurance Commissioner, new data show decreasing property insurance premiums in the first six months of 2026 in 51 of 67 counties, including all five counties in the WPTV viewing area.WATCH BELOW: Decreasing homeowners insurance? State data says yesThe July 2026 Property Insurance Stability Report from January 2026 to July 2026 showed the following average premiums:Palm Beach County: $6,412 to $6,323, which is a decrease of 1.4%Martin County: $5,993 to $5,899, which is a decrease of 1.6%St. Lucie County: $3,522 to $3,491, which is a decrease of 0.9%Indian River County: $4,453 to $4,334, which is a decrease of 2.7%Okeechobee County: $3,754 to $3,730, which is a decrease of 0.6%The report cited reduced litigation from state reforms as one of the main drivers in lowering rates for many insurers. For many, the reductions may seem modest, and for others, relief is still not being seen. "It has been going up, never went down," Barry Garcia, a Palm Beach County resident, said. Palm Beach County Commissioner Gregg Weiss, who dropped wind coverage on his West Palm Beach home several years ago, said he's saved tens of thousands of dollars. Experts said dropping insurance coverage carries risks, especially if a damaging storm hits, and it's an option available only to homeowners who don't have a mortgage. He said he and other county commissioners still hear from residents about high insurance costs. "One of the big ticket items of living here is the cost of homeowners insurance," Weiss said.

A Florida couple who had both flood and homeowners insurance before the 2024 hurricane season says the money they received from their insurer and FEMA was nowhere close to enough to rebuild. They shared their story, still standing on an empty lot nearly two years later.'IT JUST CAME IN TOO FAST'Jen and RJ Garbowicz lost their home first to flooding during Hurricane Helene, then had roof damage in Hurricane Milton."It was coming in through the floor, coming in through the walls. I actually got electrocuted a couple of times," RJ said.He said he ultimately had no choice but to stop trying to save the home."So I called it quits. I can't keep up," he said.Then 13 days later, water poured in again through the roof as Hurricane Milton took force.RELATED STORY | Is your home covered? Why summer is peak season for insurance claims 'WE DID ALL THE RIGHT THINGS'The couple paid between $18,000 and $20,000 a year for both flood and homeowners insurance. They are still in legal discussions with their homeowners insurance company over one claim.Their flood insurance, through FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program, paid out the maximum of $250,000."Which is great," Jennifer said.But RJ added that the couple is only getting $50,000 of that to rebuild, "Because we had a mortgage, they took the money, and they're holding it."FEMA also required the couple to rebuild under the 50% rule. The $250,000 payout was nowhere near enough to cover demolition and rebuilding. They turned to FEMA for additional help."I appealed four times by sending the same documentation over and over, and finally, after the fourth time, I got an approval, so we got a total of 33,000," Jennifer said.That FEMA disaster grant approval was not nearly enough. So the couple turned to an SBA loan. But the money there is being withheld too."Well, you have to first cover the difference between what insurance monies you received and the total cost of the build and subtract out the loan. So you have to cover the gap with your own cash," RJ said.And then the couple said that before they could receive an SBA disaster loan they had qualified for, they now had to repay that $33,000 grant to FEMA."It's really unfortunate that we did all the right things. We took all the right steps. We had insurance, we did everything as homeowners that we were supposed to do, and at the end of the day when we were counting on it, it didn't work like we thought that it would," Jennifer said.AVERAGE FEMA PAYOUTIn June, the Scripps News Group's Nadeen Yanes traveled to an insurance workshop where Florida Emergency Management Director Kevin Guthrie spoke as a guest. Guthrie also served on the President's FEMA Review Council. He nearly urged insurance companies to make sure policyholders understand that FEMA will not make homeowners whole."Let's just be very, very candid. The average person is going to get a $4,500 payout from this, from FEMA," Guthrie said.FIGHTING FOR FEMA REFORMThe Garbowicz traveled to Washington, D.C., as part of the Extreme Weather Survivors group to push for both FEMA and insurance reform."Everyone here today knows that disasters don't end when the news coverage does," a speaker at the event said."The important thing for us was just to get the conversation going, get the message out there," RJ said.The couple met with lawmakers to advocate for the FEMA Act, a House proposal that would completely reform the agency. Key provisions of the bill include:Makes FEMA and independent agency by removing FEMA from under the Department of Homeland SecurityCreating a universal application process for disaster recoveryProcessing FEMA grants faster, providing money to homeowners before recovery rather than as reimbursementFacilitates investment, mitigation efforts, and damage prevention before a storm hitsRELATED STORY | The hidden risk in your insurance policy: Why state minimums may not save you'WE NEED LONG-TERM SOLUTIONS'"Long-term disaster recovery, as you can see, doesn't end a day, a week, a month, or even in this case a year after the storm. It's many, many years of recovery, and we need long-term solutions," said one of the speakers at the Extreme Weather Survivors group in DC.The couple says those reforms would have helped them rebuild sooner, instead of still standing on an empty lot nearly two years after the storms. They estimate they have another 18 to 24 months of rebuilding ahead."It's been a long time coming, two years, and we probably still have another 18 to 24 months still left," RJ said."The important thing for us was just to get the conversation going, get the message out there," Jennifer added. "Just tell our story as much as possible because I think that's what it's going to take. It's going to take interviews like this, getting out there and really putting pressure."This story was originally published by Nadeen Yanes with the Scripps News Group in Tampa.

New numbers show a growing gap between retiring in South Florida and retiring on the state's Gulf Coast.A report from the online website 24/7 Wall St. said a retiree on Florida's Gulf Coast needs roughly $550,000 in invested assets to fund retirement versus $1.15 million for the same lifestyle on the state's Atlantic Coast.WATCH BELOW: Report: Florida retirees face $600K cost difference between coasts "It seems like a lot of the dynamics in Florida, particularly around insurance and housing costs, have really made it a Gulf Coast versus Atlantic conversation," financial publisher Austin Smith of 24/7 Wall St. The report looked at many retirement factors such as housing, insurance, food, utilities, transportation and healthcare. "Our math was based on a three-bedroom home fairly close to the water," Smith said. "If you moved to a place like Delray Beach or Stuart, your costs to simply live in that location could jump by as much as $20,000 a year, driven almost entirely by wind and flood coverage and additional higher property taxes." Property taxes are a big issue in Florida, with voters deciding on a referendum this November to raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills. Opponents of the referendum say cutting property taxes will only lead to raising other fees and taxes to maintain public safety and local services. "It's always been a snowbird state, but not everybody can make that southeastern move work," Smith said.

Amendment 3 has new wording, but the same policy.Attorney General James Uthmeier released a court-ordered rewrite Thursday, 10 days after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank ruled that the original title and summary were biased, misleading and inaccurate.WATCH BELOW: Florida releases court-ordered rewrite of Amendment 3 First reported by the Tampa Bay Times, the new title, "Increased Homestead Exemption; Lower Cap on Increases in Non-Homestead Property Assessments," replaces "Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes," which Frank called more of a political slogan than a neutral description.The rewrite also removes claims that the amendment "benefits" taxpayers, "protects small businesses," "ensures" core services and guarantees "fairness" for Florida residents.Instead, it spells out the mechanics.The measure would raise the homestead exemption for non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments after that. The old language only mentioned the $250,000 exemption, even though it would not take effect until the second year.The rewrite also makes clear there is no required schedule to eliminate non-school homestead property taxes. Lawmakers would instead create a process allowing local governments to raise the exemption further, potentially up to a home's full assessed value.It also says the annual assessment-growth cap would drop from 10% to 5% for all non-homestead property, including rentals, vacation homes and commercial buildings, not just small businesses.New Florida residents would receive the existing exemption after qualifying for homestead, but would not receive the larger exemption until their fifth year of claiming it.Former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes, a plaintiff in one of the consolidated challenges, welcomed the rewrite."Finally, the practicing attorneys took control of the language," Brandes said in a text. "The text is honest about what the amendment does. I hope Florida voters will dig deeper, ask hard questions, and understand the consequences before they decide the outcome."Opponents say the clearer language does not fix what they consider a flawed proposal."The revised ballot language in response to the court's ruling more accurately represents the underlying policy for voters," Florida Policy Institute CEO Sadaf Knight said. "However, the amendment’s harmful potential impacts remain the same."State analysts estimate the measure would eventually reduce recurring local property-tax revenue by nearly $12 billion annually. Opponents warn that could mean service cuts or higher taxes and fees elsewhere."The language on voters' ballots may have changed, but Amendment 3 is still a scam and a tax shift," said Jackson Peel, communications director for Save Our Services–No on 3.Gov. Ron DeSantis, who pushed the proposal, argues homeowners need relief from rapidly rising local property-tax collections and local governments can rein in spending.Amendment 3 needs at least 60% support to pass in November. If approved, it would take effect Jan.

The All-Star Game is returning to San Francisco in two years.Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred made the announcement Friday that the 2028 Midsummer Classic will be at Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. The 2007 game was played in the picturesque waterfront ballpark, featuring Hall of Famer Ichiro Suzuki's famous inside-the-park home run that bounced off the tricky wall in right-center field.“With its passionate fanbase, world-class ballpark, and rich baseball history, San Francisco will be an outstanding host for All-Star Week, which culminates in one of Major League Baseball’s best traditions, the Midsummer Classic,” Manfred said in a statement. "We look forward to bringing the excitement of All-Star Week and the celebration of baseball to the Bay Area.”This will mark another major sporting event for the Bay Area recently after the Super Bowl and World Cup this year and the NBA All-Star Game in February 2025.The Giants will host the Midsummer Classic for a fourth time overall after Candlestick Park held the first All-Star Game of the 1961 season and also baseball's summer showcase in 1984.RELATED STORY | MLB restricts dugout iPad use to prevent use of AI to make decisionsOracle Park is set to become the eighth active ballpark to hold the All-Star Game multiple times, joining Fenway Park in 1946, 1961 and 1999, Wrigley Field (1947, 1962, 1990), Angel Stadium (1967, 1989, 2010), Dodger Stadium (1980, 2022), Progressive Field (1997, 2019), Coors Field (1998, 2021) and T-Mobile Park (2001, 2023).Giants President and CEO Larry Baer said the club is “incredibly honored” and expressed his gratitude.“This is a tremendous opportunity to showcase our organization, our city, and the incredible passion of our fans on baseball’s biggest summer stage,” he said in a statement.RELATED STORY | Survey: 38% of Americans support MLB's automated balls and strikes system“Hosting the All-Star Game is more than celebrating the game’s brightest stars, it’s a chance to highlight the people, neighborhoods, and culture that make our community so special. Few cities offer the unique combination of sports, culture, innovation, entertainment, and natural beauty that defines San Francisco. We look forward to welcoming players, families, fans, and visitors from around the world for a week that will create lasting memories and have a meaningful impact throughout our region.”

Ever wonder what it is like to be a professional athlete, especially off the field? Several high school football teams got an inside look on Saturday at the Miami Dolphins High School Media Day.Schools from across South Florida came to Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens for a day packed full of activities.“I think the activities are pretty fun,” said senior wide receiver from Boca Raton High School Keston Dokes.At media day, players smiled big for their professional headshot, tried out virtual reality football and even went through a mock press conference. Teams also sat in on presentations about sportsmanship and mental health.“You know, I didn't expect to come here and like to talk about mental health, but it's pretty beneficial. “We are more than football players as to when we went to the mental health section over here, she said, ' Take off your helmet and your jersey. Paige O'Donnell has relinquished the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed with WPTV on Friday, clearing the way for the dogs to be adopted or fostered once they are healthy enough.WATCH BELOW: Deputies describe 'the filth' involved in rescuing 36 neglected dogsO'Donnell faces 72 charges in what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case it has ever seen. The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month. A WPTV investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe into the case.Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."WATCH BELOW: Healing begins for animals rescued in Martin County hoarding casesThe Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal.Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."WATCH BELOW: 'Worst case we've ever seen': Humane Society caring for 36 rescued dogsPerea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under the law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said communities should watch for several warning signs that animal hoarding may be occurring nearby."The smell will probably be your first indicator," Perea said. "If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that's also a big indicator."Perea said the situation can escalate when people feel compassion for animals but lack the resources to properly care for them."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," Perea said.The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued Border Collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation. The shelter is also asking for donations to its emergency medical fund or through its Amazon Wish List.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County Fire District board met today to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation. After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it. The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing. Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying, "It was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate." Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September. Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. Multiple people were hospitalized Thursday morning after a school bus collided with a pickup truck just south of Greenacres, according to Palm Beach County Fire Rescue.The crash happened around 6:35 a.m. at the intersection of West Lantana Road and Plantation Boulevard in front of Palm Beach Plantation. Joaquín García High School were on the bus at the time, and none of them were taken to the hospital.However, all four people in the truck suffered serious injuries and required rescue efforts to free them from the wreckage. They were all taken to a local trauma center.Nineteen different fire rescue units responded to the scene. Fire rescue crews arrived within four minutes of the initial 911 call and began treating the trapped victims even before they could be freed from the vehicle."The last person was out of the vehicle at about 7:20 a.m., so it was an extensive extrication," said Capt. Tom Reyes with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. "There were other people that came out sooner than that, but this was this was a significant incident. We had our special operations teams come here, and they went right to work working on it. More importantly, we did start with patient care even before they were out of the vehicle."The cause of the crash remains under investigation by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Reyes said it's unclear what led to the collision.The eastbound lanes of Lantana Road near Plantation Boulevard remain closed while authorities conduct their investigation, with westbound traffic reduced to two lanes. Officials advise drivers to avoid the area for the remainder of the morning as the investigation is expected to be lengthy.The school district has contacted the families of all students involved. Below is the statement sent to all families of Dr. Joaquín García High School:"Good morning, Dr. Joaquín García High School families, I am writing to inform you that Bus CO48 was transporting ten students when it was involved in a traffic crash this morning near Lantana Road and Hagen Ranch Road.All ten students on board are safe and did not require medical intervention on scene of the crash. They were transported to school and met directly by our school nurse to check on their well-being when they arrived at school. Emergency medical services and School Police responded to the school to assist.Because experiencing an incident like this can be unsettling, counseling resources and support services are available on campus today for any student who may need to speak about their experience."

A Miami woman was arrested in Martin County after allegedly posing as a bank representative to scam residents out of thousands of dollars, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. Newly released aerial footage shows sheriff's deputies following the suspect, 32-year-old Monquie Turnbull, on I-95 before stopping her vehicle. Body camera footage captured Turnbull exiting her car and being questioned by deputies. "You’re going to be placed under arrest," a deputy said in the footage. Budensiek said Turnbull drove from Miami to Martin County, where she approached two residents, claiming their debit cards were compromised and needed to be turned in for replacement. "They stated that their card was compromised and they needed to turn their card in and they were going to replace their card for them," Budensiek said. One resident was scammed out of hundreds of dollars. "The victim notices pretty quick that not long after the suspect left, there’s $3,180 now missing from her account," Budensiek said. While investigators were handling that case, they received a second 911 call matching the suspect’s description and vehicle. Deputies began their search. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "She was located as she came eastbound on Bridge Road and then she turned around and was going westbound on Bridge Road, which is the video you saw her getting arrested," Budensiek said. Officials later discovered Turnbull had entered the jail with about $3,200 hidden in one of her body parts. "She took our first victim’s card, withdrew $3,180, and that’s the exact amount recovered from inside her person in the jail," Budensiek said. The sheriff urged residents to be cautious if someone comes to their home claiming to be from a bank and asking for credit cards. "This particular incidence, this was all the money that this lady had, this was her rent money, it was everything that she had, and she handed it over to a scammer," Budensiek said. The sheriff is asking anyone who may have been a victim to contact authorities. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

For some families, finding the right place for their children to learn, grow and connect can be a challenge. Lucie organization is bringing together music, art, dance and therapy — creating a space where students of all abilities can find their voice.WATCH BELOW: House of Music PSL opens doors for students of all abilitiesStephen Lepore has been part of the House of Music PSL since 2021, when he first joined as a student. Now, he works there as a program assistant."My name is Stephen Lepore and I'm from right here in Port St. Lucie, but many of my friends call me Mr. Hollywood," Lepore said."As a program assistant I help put the staff organize stuff, helping people get ready for class," Lepore said.He plays piano and drums and was preparing a song for an upcoming Christmas recital."House of Music, they always make me feel welcomed, they always make me feel right at home," Lepore said.That feeling of belonging is something families say they find throughout the House of Music. Ashley Aguirre first came to the organization about two years ago, looking for a speech therapist for her daughter, Alia."We started with speech classes for her, then she started the early education music group classes and that allowed her, because I'm a stay-at-home mom and a homeschooler, for her to get some fellowship," Aguirre said.Alia now takes piano and ballet, and her younger brother has joined the music group classes, too."Listening to a teacher that's not mom, so all of us. It's really been such a blessing and an answered prayer for the whole family," Aguirre said.That sense of connection extends to students with special needs. Johnny Ortiz is nonverbal and has mobility disabilities. After aging out of other services at 21, his mom, Jenifer, brought him to the House of Music."Having somebody who actually believes in him, because they push him to the limits and seeing how much he's grown," Jenifer said.She says the progress can show up in ways big and small — even something as simple as throwing a ball."I tried playing ball with him all the time and I would throw at him and the ball would just roll over, and I don't know what Lucas did, but now he throws back and forth," Jenifer said."The high fives and all that, that really helps him," Jenifer said.For founder Maive Arndt, the House of Music wasn't the plan. After decades as a music teacher and therapist in Brazil, she moved to the United States with her family, expecting to only stay a year."This is not easy, especially for me. I was 43 years old when we moved here and start from zero with language, the culture," Arndt said.She says she tried to find work in music, but doors kept closing. In 2017, she and her family took a chance and opened the House of Music PSL."The families start to ask us, you need to do other things because my kids want to stay here," Arndt said.Today, its programs reach children and adults through music, dance, art, speech, special-needs services and sports."We think about our families, we think about our kids…we work with so much love," Arndt said.For the families there, that love has made them feel seen, supported and celebrated."They believe in him, sometimes more than I do, which is amazing. I feel like they're family," Jenifer said.House of Harmony is their nonprofit organization. The nonprofit is committed to providing access to music and arts education, offering community programs and outreach, supporting neurodivergent individuals through music therapy and creating inclusive and inspiring learning environments. A man the Martin County Sheriff's Office referred to as a "brazen" robber is now facing felony charges, accused of a jewelry theft at the Treasure Coast Mall. It happened at Royal Jewelers, a kiosk inside the mall, on July 20. Security video from the mall shows a man standing at the counter of the kiosk. Chris Morales of the Martin County Sheriff’s Office identified the man as 25-year-old Dezmone Johnson. "He actually comes up and pretends to be a customer, engages with the clerk for a few minutes," Morales said. According to Morales, Johnson walked away at one point before returning to ask for a closer look at the jewelry. "The clerk brings out a tray of, let's say, seven or eight less expensive necklaces according to him, and he just grabs the tray and runs out," Morales said. The clerk at the store can be heard screaming as the suspect runs away with the necklaces. According to the police report, the necklaces are valued between $850 and $4,500 each, totaling more than $22,000 in stolen jewelry. Cameras outside the mall showed investigators the vehicle Johnson drove away in. "We were able to get the tag from that vehicle, making it pretty easy for us. The vehicle came back to an address in Lauderhill, so down in Broward County," Morales said. Detectives visited a pawn shop near the Lauderhill address and stopped in to ask if Johnson was a customer. "Lo and behold, the owner says, 'Yeah, he was just in here trying to pawn a few necklaces.' Again, making it pretty easy for our detectives," Morales said. Johnson was arrested shortly afterward. Morales expressed relief at the arrest, saying even though this specific robbery was not violent, the next one might have been. "I would say there's a great chance of that. He has a history of violence. He has access to weapons in his criminal history. I'm sure he's not afraid to use that in future endeavors," Morales said. Johnson is charged with robbery and grand theft. He spent a short time in the Broward County jail and is currently free on bond as he awaits trial. A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel, ending a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in Indian River County. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures, according to the sheriff's office. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide. Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. "She had actually told her co-workers, 'If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him, I'm not here,'" Flowers said. "She had broken things off with him, he had moved away and somehow she knew that he could potentially be coming to the area." WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers gives update on Vero Beach homicide arrest According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from an unknown location to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning. "You see that video of him walking, he was dropped off around the corner, he made his way in, we've got him on video, on Ring doorbells, on a variety of different security cameras," Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators. The sheriff's office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle's movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. "At this moment, we don't have charges on her, but we are actively speaking with her," Flowers said. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife, according to the sheriff's office. Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. "I'm not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia," Flowers said. "So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this." The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic's body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night — a timeline Flowers called "unbelievable police work." Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement. Waggle will be extradited back to Indian River County to face the first-degree murder charge.
