Small business owners and longtime residents are raising concerns that rising commercial rents along Delray Beach's Atlantic Avenue are threatening the mom-and-pop shops that help define the popular downtown corridor, according to business owners and community members who contacted WPTV.Gail DelVecchio, a Delray Beach resident who has visited the area for decades and lived there full-time for the past four years, said she reached out to WPTV because she fears the trend could undermine the character that makes Atlantic Avenue a destination."They've done such a great job bringing it back," DelVecchio said. It's just a great happening place and I hate to see that ruined."WATCH:Amanda Perna, owner of boutique A Little Wild on Atlantic Avenue, shared similar concerns in an email to WPTV. Perna said tenants who have operated businesses on the strip for a decade are being pushed out due to rent increases.The issue comes as Delray Beach's downtown continues to attract visitors and new development, potentially creating pressure on commercial real estate prices. The city's Downtown Development Authority reports that 95% of shops on Atlantic Avenue are classified as small businesses, making rent affordability a critical factor for the corridor's future.The Downtown Development Authority (DDA) acknowledges that business operating costs are rising but says rent increases are not the only factor behind recent business closures along the avenue. However, the authority was unable to provide WPTV with specific data on average commercial rent costs along Atlantic Avenue or the current number of vacant storefronts. According to the DDA, many empty commercial spaces along Atlantic Avenue are currently undergoing renovations by new tenants, and overall commercial vacancy rates remain low compared to other cities in South Florida.The city and Downtown Development Authority continue to monitor the situation as they work to balance economic growth with preserving the small-business character that defines much of Atlantic Avenue's appeal.Small business owners or employees on Atlantic Avenue are welcome to share their stories— email Victor Jorges at victor.jorges@wptv.com.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The man accused of grabbing an entire display of gold chains from a jewelry kiosk at Treasure Coast Square Mall and fleeing on foot has been arrested and has already bonded out of jail, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . According to the sheriff's office, the robbery happened July 20 at the Royal Jewelers kiosk near the mall's main entrance in Jensen Beach. Investigators say a man approached the counter and asked to see several gold chains, trying some on before handing them back and walking away. He briefly left the mall, then returned and told the employee his girlfriend thought the chains he'd looked at were too expensive, asking to see cheaper options. When the employee pulled out a new display holding 9 gold chains, deputies say the man suddenly grabbed the entire display out of her hands and ran. He fled through the same entrance he'd come in, past a Ruby Tuesday and Port Barna Restaurant, and got into a silver Ford Fusion that was later seen on nearby surveillance video heading south on Federal Highway. The sheriff's office says the stolen merchandise was worth more than $22,000. Three of the necklaces were later recovered, two of them found on the ground near the mall's south exit, leaving six chains valued at roughly $13,000 still missing. Investigators say a Sheriff's Office crime scene unit lifted fingerprints and palm prints from the glass display counter where the suspect had been handling the chains, along with DNA from necklaces he tried on and a pair of sunglasses that fell off while he was running. Deputies say those prints matched 25-year-old Dezmone Karlde' Rome Johnson of Lauderhill. The sheriff's office says Johnson already had an open felony warrant out for a probation violation at the time of the robbery. Investigators say he was also spotted the following day at a Broward County pawn shop with a woman who may have pawned one of the stolen chains. An arrest warrant was approved and filed in the Martin County case, and Johnson was taken into custody July 31 by the Broward County Sheriff's Office with the help of the U.S. Marshals Fugitive Task Force. He recently bonded out of the Broward County Jail on separate charges. Sheriff John Budensiek explains why the arrest came more than a week after the robbery. "The next day, we had fingerprints from our suspect. Immediately we had a tag from the car in a description, but we wanted to kind of put it all together and do it the right way, as opposed to hastily running out and making an arrest that could or could not be beat in a court," said Budensiek. See also: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The sheriff described Johnson as having an extensive criminal history, including prior arrests involving firearms charges and resisting. "He's been through the system, but he's used to the revolving door system," Budensiek said. "That's not going to be the case here. If you steal $22,000 worth of anything from one of our Martin County businesses or residences, the 19th Circuit will lock you up, and you're likely to do prison time here in our circuit." Budensiek said Johnson will face the Martin County charges in addition to the felony probation violation warrant out of Broward County, and said investigators don't yet know why Johnson specifically targeted the Treasure Coast Square Mall. He also cautioned that mall kiosks like Royal Jewelers can be especially vulnerable, since they typically have fewer security cameras and safeguards than storefront businesses, and said this year alone the mall has seen multiple snatch-and-grab incidents targeting kiosks. He encouraged vendors to ask for identification or proof of funds from customers requesting to see high-value merchandise.

The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrest of Matthew Waggle in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewic on First Street in Vero Beach early Sunday morning. Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewic and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation. “He was there for 10, 15 minutes tops. He murdered her in cold blood in the street,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a news conference. Flowers said Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle to her co-workers at a hair salon. “She had actually told her co-workers out at the hair salon, ‘If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I’m not here,’” Flowers said. The sheriff credited the controversial Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle. “Without Flock, I’m not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia. So for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system,” Flowers said. Waggle was found at a motel in West Virginia, and officials said the gun used in the shooting belonged to Waggle’s ex-wife. “She was at the hotel, the same hotel that we got him at. So they were definitely in communication. We don’t know to what extent, what she knew. We don’t know if she knew his plans. All those are things that our detectives will be asking,” Flowers said. The sheriff added that Waggle’s ex-wife is still being questioned and is not currently facing any charges. Marshals took a person of interest into custody Wednesday night in connection with the shooting death of a 52-year-old woman in Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced. Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian, was arrested at a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia. Detectives are working to return him to Indian River County. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office identified the victim as Dawn Kriskewic . Investigators are treating her death as a domestic violence homicide. At approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday, the sheriff's office received a 911 call reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street. Deputies located Kriskewic with an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. She was transported to a trauma center, where she was later pronounced dead. Detectives and crime scene personnel processed the scene outside the victim's home. Sheriff Eric Flowers identified Waggle as the person of interest and said investigators believe Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship and that he fled the area in a vehicle following the shooting. Flowers called the incident a tragedy and said detectives used resources such as Flock cameras to investigate Waggle's whereabouts. "At this point we're not sure, but this could be a domestic violence incident. It's a loss of life that's so unnecessary," Flowers said. "So our team is committed to working on that." Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home. "My brother actually heard the shot," Cardenas said. "So he went inside to check on my sister." Cardenas said the neighborhood is typically quiet. "Nothing like this should happen, especially in quiet neighborhoods," Cardenas said. Cardenas said he hopes an arrest comes soon. "I just hope that they find the suspect," Cardenas said. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Kachele at 772-978-6240 or mkachele@ircsheriff.org , or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers. Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. FORT PIERCE – The Fort Pierce City Commission Monday said no for the third time to a proposal to settle a citizen lawsuit over the Little Jim Bait and Tackle property. Commissioner Arnold Gaines, himself an attorney, suggested that a settlement demand that Little Jim’s current operator be given the right to match the outcome of any future bids to lease the city-owned property, would violate state law. Public entities are required to competitively bid the awarding of things like property leases to get the best outcome for taxpayers. Gaines suggested giving Little Jim’s current operator an automatic “right of first refusal” would violate the principle of competitive bidding. Instead, commissioners unanimously decided to offer a counter settlement that says they are willing to forgo a claim for the city’s legal costs involved in defending the lawsuit – a minimum $3,600 – if plaintiff Kevin Keene will drop his action. Keene, a Fort Pierce resident, said he filed suit against the city in October as an attempt to give citizens more authority in determining how city-owned waterfront property is used. Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. The current operator, Salty Baitshack 3, has continued business there on a month-to-month lease for more than a year. Lucie County judge has twice dismissed Keene’s lawsuit, but gave him an opportunity to refile. Keene’s latest settlement offer would: – Require the city to suspend any new Requests for Proposals (RFP) for awarding the next long-term Little Jim lease until all issues with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection have been resolved. – Require the city to agree to put any future sale or long-term lease of publicly owned waterfront property to a citywide vote. – Give Little Jim’s current operator the right to match the highest bid resulting from an RFP process. A new lease would be for no more than nine years and the property would be leased “in its existing ‘as-is’ condition, without requiring or conditioning the new lease upon any additional improvements, alterations, redevelopment, or other changes to the property.” Your comment has been submitted. The sheriff’s office said its deputies are at the scene searching for the source of the gunfire, and at this time, there is no indication that a crime occurred, but that could change as the search continues. An overwhelming number of people have posted comments on WPTV's Facebook page, calling for the death penalty for suspended Palm Beach County clerk Mike Caruso following his arrest on alleged sexual abuse charges, so we're getting answers.The question of whether the suspended Palm Beach County Clerk and Comptroller could face the death penalty comes down to the details of how a state law is written — and whether his charges qualify him for it.WATCH BELOW: Could Mike Caruso face death penalty? Ron DeSantis, who appointed Caruso, weighed in on the possibility of the death penalty after the arrest."We're the first state to reintroduce the death penalty for pedophiles, and I'm proud that I signed that into law and I'm proud that we have very strong penalties for people that abuse children and if he's convicted he's going to be in a world of hurt," DeSantis said.DeSantis was referring to the 2023 Florida Capital Sexual Battery Law — a law Caruso himself voted in favor of when he was a state representative. The law allows prosecutors to seek the death penalty for adults convicted of sexually battering a child under the age of 12.Caruso was arrested on five felony charges related to child sex abuse, including kidnapping, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious exhibition, luring or enticing a child, and child abuse causing mental injury. The alleged victim was between 3 and 5 years old.The challenge is that Caruso has not been charged with sexual battery. Without that charge, the law that could put him on death row does not currently apply to him.But that could change. On Tuesday, Attorney General James Uthmeir said more charges are expected. Caruso appeared in court Thursday in shackles and was issued no bond in Orange County, where he will go before a judge in a couple of weeks. At that point, the state could add a capital sexual battery charge — which could then potentially qualify Caruso for the death penalty.WPTV spoke with Caruso's attorney, Jason Weiss, after Caruso appeared at his first appearance in Palm Beach County on Wednesday. Weiss said his client is innocent and that Caruso intends to "vigorously" defend himself against these charges.The victim's attorney, Lisa Haba, said the family is completely shattered. Court documents show the boy has been receiving therapy.When asked whether the family was considering pushing for the death penalty — given that Caruso himself once supported it — Haba did not commit to an answer."I don't have an answer for that," Haba said.But she made clear the toll this has taken on the child."He never asked for any of this to happen to him. Now the child that was harmed in this case is going to be on a healing journey for probably the rest of his life," Haba said.And she said the family's focus right now is on accountability."The family and the victim want justice; they want accountability for what happened," Haba said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A Florida investor tells Scripps News Group Tampa Bay reporter Michael Paluska that artificial intelligence has become his most valuable business partner — one that never takes a day off, never calls in sick, and never asks for a paycheck.Alex Jandick, owner of 131 Cash Home Buyers in St. Petersburg, says he now relies on an AI agent called Claude to handle nearly every administrative task in his one-person operation — from marketing to bookkeeping — saving him more than $41,000 a year.Before making the switch, Jandick was paying $2,500 a month for marketing and nearly $1,000 a month for a bookkeeper."Did you tell them that you replaced them with AI?" Paluska asked."Nope. I just let them go," Jandick said.Claude currently handles both for $100 a month."So what does Claude do now for the marketing side?" Paluska asked."Everything, everything that I tell it to," Jandick said. "I sit in my office, and I tell a robot, Claude, what to do."After spending about two weeks setting up and fine-tuning the system, Jandick said the results were immediate."It's like holy smokes! This is — it was everything that I had wanted to get done at a cheaper rate for a year," Jandick said.Now, Jandick says he and Claude essentially split the workload. A human still has to verify the information and input the correct prompts. But the AI takes it from there."I put in 25 to 30 hours a week, and I have Claude probably putting in 25 to 30 hours a week," Jandick said.Jandick is the sole employee of his company, meaning no workers were displaced when he made the switch. Still, after posting online about his AI-driven savings, he faced criticism."I get that there's going to be haters out there," Jandick said.He pushed back directly."I'm saving $41,000 per year; for me, that is an incredible amount of money. That's my kids' college savings funds."The broader question of how many jobs AI could eliminate remains unsettled. According to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report, AI will displace 92 million jobs globally by 2030. However, the same report projects 170 million new roles will open up — a net gain of 78 million jobs worldwide. A separate 2026 Goldman Sachs study estimates 300 million jobs globally are exposed to automation by AI, though that research did not cite specific numbers for job gains.For Jandick, the technology has changed more than just his bottom line. He said he used to feel isolated working alone. Now, he tells Paluska, that has changed."Before Claude, I did get lonely," Jandick said. Now, I wake up in the morning with a bit more energy. I'm more excited because it's like I don't have to work so hard to break even each month. You know, it does take a little bit of legwork to get all set up and everything, but I have not found anything that is a better cost cutter than AI at this point," Jandick said.

Lucie police arrested a man early Thursday morning after executing a search warrant at a home as part of an ongoing investigation. Thursday officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department served a search warrant at a residence in the 900 block of SW Jaslo Avenue. During the operation, Virgil Jason Vinz was taken into custody on an arrest warrant without injury. Police said Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. The police response drew attention from nearby residents, some of whom reported hearing sounds they believed were gunfire. According to the department, the noises were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices, commonly used by SWAT teams during certain tactical operations. Authorities said the devices were deployed by the Port St. Lucie Police Department SWAT Team while officers carried out the warrant. The department emphasized that the case remains an active and ongoing investigation. Additional information is expected to be released when authorities determine it is appropriate. A man accused of traveling to Indian River County with the intent to kill his ex-girlfriend, a Vero Beach hairdresser, was captured in West Virginia after a four-day investigation that authorities say was aided by license plate reader technology. The investigation began Sunday morning, when authorities found Dawn Kriskewic’s body in a roadway in the southern part of the county. Officials said investigators initially did not know who she was and had not previously encountered her. By Wednesday night, authorities had tracked Waggle to a motel in West Virginia and taken him into custody. This has been an absolutely incredible case for them to put this together and make all of this happen in such a short amount of time, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a news conference. Authorities said Kriskewic had ended her relationship with Waggle before the shooting and had warned coworkers at the hair salon that she wanted no contact with him. She had actually told her coworkers at the hair salon, If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I’m not here,’ the sheriff said. Investigators believe Waggle traveled to the area specifically to kill Kriskewic. Waggle came here to Indian River County fully intent on shooting and killing Dawn, the sheriff said. That was his entire premise. According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus to Orlando before taking an Uber to Indian River County. Surveillance footage, including Ring doorbell video and other security cameras, captured him walking toward Kriskewic’s residence after being dropped off nearby. Authorities said Waggle and Kriskewic had a brief interaction before he shot her and fled. He walked to the residence. They had a brief interaction. He shot her, and then he fled that area, the sheriff said. Investigators said Waggle then took an Uber back to Orlando, boarded another Greyhound bus and traveled to North Carolina before eventually making his way to West Virginia. Authorities said no one appeared to have traveled with him. Investigators interviewed the Uber drivers who transported Waggle and found that he had a single bus ticket. Sheriff credits network of license plate readers The sheriff credited the agency’s Real Time Crime Center and a network of license plate readers with helping investigators piece together Waggle’s movements and locate him. For everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this, the sheriff said. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system. The sheriff clarified that Flock is one brand of automated license plate reader used by law enforcement. We’ve made so many cases, and we’ve protected this community as a result of this, and this is just another example of that, he said. Investigators also focused on Waggle’s ex-wife, who was in West Virginia and had been communicating with him. Authorities said the Real Time Crime Center determined she had been making calls to a specific motel. Investigators eventually found Waggle at that same motel. The sheriff said the gun believed to have been used in the killing belonged to Waggle’s ex-wife and that she knew he had it. Two detectives were sent to West Virginia to interview both Waggle and his ex-wife and determine how much she knew about his plans and what assistance, if any, she provided. She was at the hotel, the same hotel that we got him at, the sheriff said. So they were definitely in communication. We don’t know what extent, what she knew. We don’t know if she knew his plans. See also: Former Vero Beach Eagles secretary accused of blowing nearly $419K on guns, liquor, LEGOs No charges had been announced against the ex-wife at the time of the news conference. Authorities said the investigation remains active as detectives continue working to establish Waggle’s movements before and after the shooting, including where his trip began, how he traveled from North Carolina to West Virginia and the circumstances surrounding his stay at the motel. The sheriff also praised witnesses who came forward during the investigation, saying their cooperation helped detectives build the case. Waggle is expected to be returned to Florida, although the timing could depend on whether he agrees to extradition or challenges the process. There’s still so much more to do in this investigation, the sheriff said. We’ve got a case to build.

The man accused of grabbing an entire display of gold chains from a jewelry kiosk at Treasure Coast Square Mall and fleeing on foot has been arrested and has already bonded out of jail, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . According to the sheriff's office, the robbery happened July 20 at the Royal Jewelers kiosk near the mall's main entrance in Jensen Beach. Investigators say a man approached the counter and asked to see several gold chains, trying some on before handing them back and walking away. He briefly left the mall, then returned and told the employee his girlfriend thought the chains he'd looked at were too expensive, asking to see cheaper options. When the employee pulled out a new display holding nine to ten gold chains, deputies say the man suddenly grabbed the entire display out of her hands and ran. He fled through the same entrance he'd come in, past a Ruby Tuesday and Port Barna Restaurant, and got into a silver Ford Fusion that was later seen on nearby surveillance video heading south on Federal Highway. The sheriff's office says the stolen merchandise was worth more than $22,000. Three of the necklaces were later recovered, two of them found on the ground near the mall's south exit, leaving six chains valued at roughly $13,000 still missing. Investigators say a Sheriff's Office crime scene unit lifted fingerprints and palm prints from the glass display counter where the suspect had been handling the chains, along with DNA from necklaces he tried on and a pair of sunglasses that fell off while he was running. Deputies say those prints matched 25-year-old Dezmone Karlde' Rome Johnson of Lauderhill. The sheriff's office says Johnson already had an open felony warrant out for a probation violation at the time of the robbery. Investigators say he was also spotted the following day at a Broward County pawn shop with a woman who may have pawned one of the stolen chains. An arrest warrant was approved and filed in the Martin County case, and Johnson was taken into custody July 31 by the Broward County Sheriff's Office. He bonded out of jail August 8. See also: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? It's not yet clear which agencies were directly involved in tracking Johnson down and making the arrest; CBS12 is working to confirm those details. The Martin County Sheriff's Office has also said the case could be turned over to Broward County for additional charges related to dealing in stolen property, pending review of the pawn shop surveillance footage. CBS12 News is speaking with Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek and will provide updates when they become available.

A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel, ending a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in Indian River County.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers gives update on Vero Beach homicide arrestMatthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally.Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures, according to the sheriff's office.Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide.Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect."She had actually told her co-workers, 'If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him, I'm not here,'" Flowers said. "She had broken things off with him, he had moved away and somehow she knew that he could potentially be coming to the area."According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from West Virginia to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning."You see that video of him walking, he was dropped off around the corner, he made his way in, we've got him on video, on Ring doorbells, on a variety of different security cameras," Flowers said.The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene.After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators.The sheriff's office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle's movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location.U.S. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators."At this moment, we don't have charges on her, but we are actively speaking with her," Flowers said.Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife, according to the sheriff's office.Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest."I'm not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia," Flowers said. "So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this."The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic's body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night — a timeline Flowers called "unbelievable police work."Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement. Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. FORT PIERCE – The Fort Pierce City Commission Monday said no for the third time to a proposal to settle a citizen lawsuit over the Little Jim Bait and Tackle property. Commissioner Arnold Gaines, himself an attorney, suggested that a settlement demand that Little Jim’s current operator be given the right to match the outcome of any future bids to lease the city-owned property, would violate state law. Public entities are required to competitively bid the awarding of things like property leases to get the best outcome for taxpayers. Gaines suggested giving Little Jim’s current operator an automatic “right of first refusal” would violate the principle of competitive bidding. Instead, commissioners unanimously decided to offer a counter settlement that says they are willing to forgo a claim for the city’s legal costs involved in defending the lawsuit – a minimum $3,600 – if plaintiff Kevin Keene will drop his action. Keene, a Fort Pierce resident, said he filed suit against the city in October as an attempt to give citizens more authority in determining how city-owned waterfront property is used. Little Jim, a former military guard post that was given to the city by the Navy after World War II, has been embroiled in controversy for more than a year over claims the current operator installed unpermitted docks that encroached on state-owned property, plus issues surrounding the 2025 award of a new lease to operate the property. The current operator, Salty Baitshack 3, has continued business there on a month-to-month lease for more than a year. Lucie County judge has twice dismissed Keene’s lawsuit, but gave him an opportunity to refile. Keene’s latest settlement offer would: – Require the city to suspend any new Requests for Proposals (RFP) for awarding the next long-term Little Jim lease until all issues with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection have been resolved. – Require the city to agree to put any future sale or long-term lease of publicly owned waterfront property to a citywide vote. – Give Little Jim’s current operator the right to match the highest bid resulting from an RFP process. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." See also: Deputies arrest man, 27, accused of traveling to meet 14-year-old in Hallandale Beach Another commenter said to the chief, "I don't know how you sleep at night." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

A 37-year-old man was shot and killed after deputies say he entered a St. Lucie County home and attacked a 22-year-old man during a dispute. The shooting happened around 9 p.m. Wednesday at the Seminole Mobile Home Park. Lucie County Sheriff Richard R. Del Toro , the two men knew each other and had been involved in a dispute that included verbal arguments and threatening text messages. Investigators say the suspect, who has yet to be identified, made several threats before showing up at the home. Deputies say he knocked on the front door and was let inside before a brawl broke out. Investigators say he pushed the 22-year-old homeowner and punched him several times in the stomach. The suspect was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. "It's not fair, 'cause my son has no father now. He's five years old, and what am I gonna tell him? We didn't even get to say goodbye," said Naomi Pallarez, the girlfriend of the man who died. The sheriff said the homeowner remained at the home and cooperated with investigators. His girlfriend and sister were also inside the home and provided statements that investigators say corroborate his account. Deputies recovered the handgun after executing a search warrant at the residence. No charges have been filed against the homeowner at this time. Investigators are working with the State Attorney's Office to determine whether the shooting falls under Florida's stand-your-ground self-defense law. "Obviously, you have to be in defense of yourself, but at the same time, you have to be in fear for your life anytime you're gonna use deadly force," Sheriff Del Toro explained. Del Toro said investigators are still reviewing evidence, including text messages between the two men. The sheriff said the suspect had a criminal history, including drug-related and resisting-officer charges, domestic violence-related charges, and three felony convictions. He stressed that the man's criminal history was not a reason for him to be killed. The suspect's name has not been released because investigators have not yet notified his next of kin and they have not released the name of the man who was killed. "I am very much heartbroken. And now I'm a single mom," Pallarez said. The sheriff said there is no known threat to the surrounding community and described the shooting as an isolated incident. Del Toro urged anyone who receives threats and believes a situation could escalate to contact law enforcement before violence occurs. "I just wish that we'd gotten involved sooner rather than being reactive and called after the fact," Del Toro said. "Could've had a different outcome."

Marshals took a person of interest into custody Wednesday night in connection with the shooting death of a 52-year-old woman in Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced. Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian, was arrested at a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia. Detectives are working to return him to Indian River County. "At this point we're not sure, but this could be a domestic violence incident. It's a loss of life that's so unnecessary," Flowers said. "So our team is committed to working on that." Marco Cardenas, a longtime resident of the area, said his siblings live in the complex and were shaken by the shooting near their home. "My brother actually heard the shot," Cardenas said. Cardenas said he hopes an arrest comes soon. "I just hope that they find the suspect," Cardenas said. Anyone with information is asked to contact Det. Florida voters’ reputation of bucking the national trend of automatically reelecting incumbents proved particularly true in Indiantown, with three incumbents swept off the Board by voters yesterday, and the county as a whole reflected a desire to restore formerly elected officials to power. That was also evident in the Primary races for three of the seats on the Stuart City Commission, an election cycle made more transformational by the April 30 resignation of Collins as then mayor of Stuart to seek the District 2 Martin County Commission vacated by Commissioner Stacey Hetherington who chose not to seek re-election. In Collins’ bid for the latter, he received 48.99 percent, or 14,657 votes, of the total 29, 916 votes cast in that race. The two other candidates, Susan O’Rourke and Althea Wiley, got 40.33 percent and 10.68 percent, respectively. In the District 2 County Commission race, Current Chairwoman and Incumbent Sarah Heard won her seventh term on the Board, with 47.53 percent, or 14,219 votes, out of a total of 29,914 cast in that race. Her challengers John Dial and John “Kaz” Kanzanjian, got 44.93 percent and 7.53 percent, respectively. The City Commission races saw a lot of intense campaigning this year, partly due to the fact that Collins’ departure left a power vacuum on that Board resulting in a series of 2-2 failed votes due to the lack of his swing slower-growth vote. His Group 3 seat, however, was claimed by former City Commissioner Merritt Matheson, who several times over the last year railed against the restrictive policies implemented by the slow-growth majority led by Collins. Matheson particularly lamented that majority’s opposition to any funding or support of a Brightline train station downtown. The chances of that possibility got slimmer this month, when Martin County did not get its desired grant funding from the state to pursue the station without the city’s help. Matheson received 58.20 percent or 2,084 votes, of the total 3,581 cast in that race. The other candidate, Derreck Ogden ran on a strictly slow-growth platform and got 41.80 percent. The Group 1 Seat Race was a lot closer, however, with Incumbent Campbell Rich getting 50.25 percent, or 1780 of the total 3,542 votes cast. His challenger, Will Laughlin, received 49.75 percent. Because the difference was just under the state-mandated 0.5 percent, a formal recount is mandatory. While Rich consistently opposed much of Collins’ and the slow-growth majority’s actions over the past few years, Laughlin ran on a platform dedicated to slowing or stopping the growth and resisting the state’s efforts at eroding home rule. If the recount affirms Rich’s victory and with Matheson’s comeback to the Board, the remaining slow-growth commissioners may find themselves in the minority in the future. As far as the Stuart Commission’s Group 5 Seat Race, incumbent Eula R. Clarke – who’s served on the Board since 2011 – received 52.12 percent or 1,867 of the total 3,582 votes cast. Her challengers Dayne Oldenborg and Kylie Micciche got 32.08 percent and 15.80 percent respectively. Both of them had run on slower-growth platforms and the preservation of local waterways. The 2026 Primary Election in the Village of Indiantown basically routed the Council of incumbents, beginning with current Mayor Carmine Dipaolo who lost Seat 3 to Challenger Christa Miley, who received 59.38 percent of the total 832 votes cast. Dipaolo himself received 32.09 percent, while Candidate Octavius Thompson got 8.53 percent. That trend continued onto the Seat 4 Race, where former Village Councilman Anthony D. Dowling received 51.59 percent or 437 of the total 847 votes cast. Incumbent Angelina Perez got 32.11 percent, while Challenger Ana Farias received 16.29 percent. Current Seat 5 Councilwoman and Incumbent Karen Onsager fared no better, losing her reelection bid to former Village Councilwoman Janet Hernandez. While Hernandez got 63.68 percent of the total 837 votes cast, Onsager got 36.32 percent. On the other hand, the three incumbents up for reelection on the Martin County School Board successfully fended off challenges to their seats. Abandoned and derelict boats are piling up at Wildcat Cove off North Hutchinson Island in Fort Pierce, and residents say the vessels are creating dangerous conditions on the water.WATCH BELOW: 'Flotilla of garbage. Needs to go,' Kevin Fitzgerald tells WPTV's Tyler HatfieldKevin Fitzgerald, who regularly navigates the waterway between Wildcat Cove and Jack Island Preserve, described to WPTV’s Tyler Hatfield what he sees on the water."It's just like a boat junkyard," Fitzgerald said.Fitzgerald counted at least 15 boats in the cove, including vessels that have sunk."I see a couple of boats ahead of me where there was just one sunk, and now there's two sunk on top of each other," he said. “There's a boat a catamaran, that's on a sandbar.”Fitzgerald said navigating the area is especially dangerous after dark."Most of them don't have lights," he said. "You come up on a boat when it's dark, it's right in front of you. You got to swerve or get out of the way. You got to watch for anchor lines and different things like that."Fitzgerald called the situation dangerous."It's like a minefield," he said.His friend Bart Plymale was also on the water and shared the same concern."It's a maze," Plymale said.Plymale said he is also worried about environmental damage from the abandoned vessels."There's fuel on these boats or oil and whatever engines that are left on them, that's all ending up in the water right now," Plymale said.WPTV went looking for answers from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.FWC said enforcement action in surrounding counties and new anchoring requirements in St. Lucie County appear to be contributing factors to the influx of boats at Wildcat Cove.FWC said it is actively investigating and that officers are in contact with at-risk vessel owners to bring their boats back into compliance. The agency said citations have been issued and vessels deemed derelict are going through the legal process before removal can be authorized.Fitzgerald said he wants the cove cleared."Flotilla of garbage. At least 15 boats," Fitzgerald said.

Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin and challenger Steven Giordano will face off in the November general election after neither candidate secured the 50% threshold needed to win outright in Tuesday’s primary race, according to election results. Martin, the incumbent mayor, captured nearly 48% of the vote while Giordano received approximately 35%, forcing a runoff between the top two candidates. Third candidate Eric Strazzeri was eliminated from the race after receiving nearly 17% of the vote. Both candidates addressed how an ongoing investigation into campaign signs may have affected Tuesday’s results. The investigation has been a focal point in the mayoral campaign leading up to the primary. “If it would’ve happened earlier, I think the results would’ve swayed better to our race,” Giordano told WPTV at his election watch party at My Brother’s BBQ, where family and friends gathered to celebrate advancing to the general election. Martin acknowledged the investigation’s potential impact during a phone interview with WFLX. “I do think that had something to do with it, but I’m going to keep focused on the issues and not on other things that are not important to the campaign,” Martin said. “I’m going to keep focusing on the issues that are important to residents and demonstrate to them how I want to continue working for them over the next four years.” Martin, who has served as Port St. Lucie’s mayor, said she plans to let her track record with the city speak to voters as the campaign moves forward. The incumbent emphasized her experience leading the city and her commitment to continuing her work for residents. Giordano outlined his campaign priorities for the November race, focusing on supporting local youth programs and local businesses. I’m the people’s mayor and the people’s voice. I’m very excited to be in this position,” Giordano said. The November general election will determine who leads Port St. Lucie for the next four years. Voters will choose between Martin’s experience as the current mayor and Giordano’s vision for change in city leadership. WFLX will continue following both candidates as they campaign leading up to the November general election. Lucie County Fire District board met today to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation. After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it. The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing. Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying, "It was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate." Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September. Christopher "Doc" Collins won the open Martin County Commission District 2 seat, defeating Susan O'Rourke and Althea Wiley in Tuesday's election. Because all three candidates were Republicans and no Democrat qualified for the race, it was held as a Universal Primary Contest, meaning Tuesday's vote decided the seat outright with no November general election to follow. Collins received 14,657 votes, or about 49 percent. O'Rourke received 12,065 votes, about 40 percent, and Wiley received 3,194 votes, nearly 11 percent. Collins, a chiropractor and former Stuart city commissioner and mayor, stepped down from the Stuart City Commission earlier this year to run for the county seat, a move required under the city's charter before he could qualify for another elected office. He ran largely on a platform of slow growth, calling for tighter restrictions on new development across the county. During his time on the Stuart City Commission, Collins joined two other commissioners in voting to rescind the city's agreement with Brightline for a downtown train station, a position that put him at odds with O'Rourke throughout the campaign. See also: Martin, Giordano head to November runoff for PSL mayor The campaign also had a tense moment in its final week, when Collins accused a man named Jim Gallegos of stealing his campaign signs, posting a Facebook video with trail camera footage and Apple AirTag tracking he said showed Gallegos pulling one of his signs from the ground. Gallegos denied stealing anything, saying he removed roughly 30 signs for various candidates, including some of Collins', at a property owner's request. The dispute also drew in Derreck Ogden, a Stuart City Commission candidate, who publicly confronted Gallegos over the signs. Collins did not respond to CBS12's requests for an interview at any point during the campaign, and did not respond to a request for comment following the results. Collins will replace outgoing Commissioner Stacey Hetherington, who chose not to seek re-election. O'Rourke, a former traffic engineer who previously served on Stuart's Local Planning Agency, ran on managing growth and easing traffic congestion. Her candidacy became the subject of a legal dispute earlier this year after Collins filed a challenge seeking to have her removed from the ballot, arguing she was not legally a Martin County resident when she qualified. A judge dismissed that challenge in July. Wiley, an author, Realtor and chef, ran on affordability, pointing to rising housing costs and other everyday expenses facing county residents. The Brightline project remains a live issue for the incoming commission. Plans call for a roughly 10,200-square-foot station, a 660-foot platform, parking and other rail infrastructure, with completion targeted for 2029. Martin County has sought $69.3 million in federal funding for the project, and the commission is expected to keep playing a role in how it moves forward. Collins will also take office as the county braces for a possible November ballot measure, Amendment 3, which would expand the state's homestead exemption and cut into local government revenue. Commissioners previously voiced their concerns about the amendment during a public meeting in July, where the Martin County Fire Chief told the county about cuts he may have to make if the amendment passes in November.

Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. A 23-year-old Fort Pierce man is behind bars for firing a gun through a bathroom door during a domestic disturbance and fleeing before being taken into custody hours later, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said. Deputies said they responded to a home on the 1700 block of Wyoming Avenue at around 11:30 a.m. Sunday for a reported domestic disturbance. During the incident, the victim locked herself inside a bathroom. Hsu allegedly fired a round through the bathroom door before fleeing the residence in a car. Fort Pierce police later located the car near Porpoise Beach, prompting an extensive search of the area. While the search was underway, detectives with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators said they executed a search warrant at the residence. At around 2:30 p.m., Hsu's family located him and alerted a passing Fort Pierce police officer. Hsu was taken into custody without incident and a firearm was recovered. Hsu is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on no bond. He faces multiple felony charges, including attempted felony murder, kidnapping, tampering with a witness, simple battery and grand theft of a motor vehicle. Authorities said the incident was isolated and there is no ongoing threat to the public. The investigation remains active.

A Florida woman took a scam beyond the phone lines, showing up at a Martin County resident’s door pretending to represent a bank and demanding the victim’s credit card on Monday. According to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office , Monique Love Turnbull, of Miami, was seen at a victim’s doorstep claiming the victim’s bank account had been compromised. Turnbull asked for the victim’s credit card and said she would dispose of it. As law enforcement investigated, deputies were alerted to another call identifying Turnbull in a separate case. Body camera video shows deputies pulling Turnbull over and asking her to step out of the car. See also: Palm Beach County clerk arrested on 5 felonies involving child, suspended by DeSantis The arresting deputy then tells Turnbull she is under arrest for fraud before placing her in handcuffs. The sheriff’s office is warning residents never to allow someone into their home if the person was not scheduled to visit. Residents should also never hand over credit cards, cash, gold or other valuables to someone who shows up unexpectedly. MCSO says anyone who comes to a resident’s home claiming to represent a bank or financial institution and asking for valuables should be treated with suspicion. Residents are urged to call 911.

A Miami woman was arrested in Martin County after allegedly posing as a bank representative to scam residents out of thousands of dollars, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. Newly released aerial footage shows sheriff's deputies following the suspect, 32-year-old Monquie Turnbull, on I-95 before stopping her vehicle. Body camera footage captured Turnbull exiting her car and being questioned by deputies. "You’re going to be placed under arrest," a deputy said in the footage. Budensiek said Turnbull drove from Miami to Martin County, where she approached two residents, claiming their debit cards were compromised and needed to be turned in for replacement. "They stated that their card was compromised and they needed to turn their card in and they were going to replace their card for them," Budensiek said. One resident was scammed out of hundreds of dollars. "The victim notices pretty quick that not long after the suspect left, there’s $3,180 now missing from her account," Budensiek said. While investigators were handling that case, they received a second 911 call matching the suspect’s description and vehicle. Deputies began their search. Officials later discovered Turnbull had entered the jail with about $3,200 hidden in one of her body parts. "She took our first victim’s card, withdrew $3,180, and that’s the exact amount recovered from inside her person in the jail," Budensiek said. The sheriff urged residents to be cautious if someone comes to their home claiming to be from a bank and asking for credit cards. "This particular incidence, this was all the money that this lady had, this was her rent money, it was everything that she had, and she handed it over to a scammer," Budensiek said. A network of license plate cameras facing growing privacy scrutiny across the country is now part of the search for a person of interest in a Vero Beach-area homicide. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers took CBS12 News Reporter Katie Bente inside the agency's Real Time Crime Center on Monday, where analysts are using Flock license plate cameras as investigators search for 33-year-old Matthew Waggle. Waggle has not been charged in the killing. Deputies identified him as a person of interest after a 52-year-old woman was found shot near her home Sunday morning in the 500 block of First Street, just outside Vero Beach. Deputies performed lifesaving measures before the woman was taken to a trauma center, where she later died. Flowers said investigators believe the woman had been trying to end a relationship with Waggle and are investigating the killing as a domestic violence homicide. On Monday, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office released 911 calls made after a bystander found the woman's body. "Is there anyone else around this female?" the 911 dispatcher can be heard asking. I didn't see nothing, because I was in my house," the caller responded. The dispatcher then asked the caller how long the woman had been there. The caller said she did not know. "One of the first places that we go, Real Time Crime Center gets activated," Flowers said. "They're looking at all the Flock cameras. They're looking at the traffic in the area." How Flock plays a role Flock's automated license plate readers capture information about vehicles as they pass, including license plates, locations and timestamps. That allows investigators to search for vehicles connected to crimes and potentially piece together where they traveled. Indian River County has previously said it operates 140 license plate readers. Flowers pointed to a deadly hit-and-run investigated by the Florida Highway Patrol last week as one recent example. He said analysts in the Real Time Crime Center used Flock data to help build a case that otherwise had no leads. He said the technology can also work in reverse helping investigators eliminate someone as a suspect. "If we're able to show that that person's vehicle was nowhere near the homicide," Flowers said, "that's a great way for us to show that somebody is innocent as well." A crime-fighting tool and a privacy fight The ability to reconstruct where vehicles have traveled is also at the heart of a growing national debate over Flock. Privacy and civil liberties advocates have questioned how extensively law enforcement should be able to track drivers, how information is shared between agencies and what safeguards exist to prevent misuse. More than 50 jurisdictions have reportedly ended relationships with Flock. The company announced new safeguards last week, including plans to reduce its recommended default data retention period from 30 days to seven days and require searches to be connected to case numbers. Flowers strongly defended Indian River County's use of the cameras. "You're on camera every time you go to Walmart. You're on camera every time you go to Walgreens," Flowers said. "Everywhere you go, your bank transactions are being tracked." Flowers said law enforcement should be able to use available technology to protect the public. "Don't you want your law enforcement protecting your community and making it safer by leveraging technology?" he said. Flowers said Indian River County has largely avoided the public backlash seen elsewhere because the Sheriff's Office explained its use of the technology early and, he argues, residents have seen results. He pointed to auto burglaries as an example, saying the county recorded more than 800 in 2015 compared with roughly 250 last year. Flowers attributed at least part of that decline to the camera network and proactive policing. Now, the technology is being used in an active homicide investigation. See also: 12 pounds of meth, 12,000 rounds,12 guns, and fentanyl found in Boynton Beach SWAT raid Flowers said investigators spent Monday speaking with the victim's coworkers and examining her relationship with Waggle as they work to determine what led to the shooting. "It really looks like she was trying to break up with him," Flowers said. He wasn't ready for it to be over." A nationwide BOLO has been issued for Waggle. Investigators have said he should be considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

That additional activity supports restaurants, hotels, shops, artists and other local businesses. FORT PIERCE — When people think about tourism in St. Lucie County, beaches, fishing, boating and spring training often come to mind. Those attractions are important, but they are only part of the story. A beach may attract someone for a day. A concert, museum, art walk, theater production or heritage trail can persuade that visitor to stay for dinner, book another night and return. That additional activity supports restaurants, hotels, shops, artists and other local businesses. Arts and culture are not simply community amenities. Lucie County’s tourism infrastructure. Lucie memorable Travelers can find beaches throughout Florida. What they cannot find everywhere is St. Lucie County’s specific collection of stories, artists and cultural experiences. Visitors can explore the legacy of the Florida Highwaymen, learn about author Zora Neale Hurston’s years in Fort Pierce, visit the A.E. Backus Museum, attend a performance at the historic Sunrise Theatre or experience local galleries, public art and live performances. Lucie’s cultural tourism offerings expanded with two free digital heritage trails. The Florida Highwaymen Heritage Trail highlights the lives and influence of the celebrated Black artists whose work helped define Florida landscape art. The Zora Neale Hurston Dust Tracks Heritage Trail connects visitors with the author’s legacy and ties to Fort Pierce. Public art installations, including The Heart in Port St. Lucie, are also being promoted as community landmarks and visitor attractions. These experiences give visitors something valuable: a sense of place. Lucie County stand apart from destinations that offer sunshine but little identity. Turning creativity into visitor experiences One of the St. Lucie Cultural Alliance’s most visible tourism-related programs is the Downtown Fort Pierce Art Walk. Artists, musicians and performers participate while galleries and businesses remain open. The event encourages people to explore downtown, meet artists, shop locally and visit nearby restaurants and businesses. The Cultural Alliance also presents many free events each year, making it easier for families, residents and visitors to explore the county’s cultural scene. Cultural visitors spend money The economic value of cultural tourism extends well beyond admission tickets. Americans for the Arts found that attendees at nonprofit arts and cultural events spend an average of $38.46 per person, per event, beyond admission. That spending includes meals, transportation, parking, shopping and other purchases. The study also found that 30.1% of arts attendees traveled from outside the county. Those visitors spent an average of $60.57 per person, compared with $29.77 spent by local attendees. Among those visitors, 77% said the cultural event was the primary reason for their trip. Those are national findings, not a measurement of St. However, they demonstrate why cultural programming matters to tourism planning. When an event attracts visitors from outside the area, the financial impact spreads through the community. Tourism is already big business St. Lucie County’s 2023 visitor tracking and economic impact report found that the county attracted approximately 1,012,800 visitors. Those visitors spent an estimated $703.8 million on accommodations, restaurants, groceries, transportation, attractions, entertainment and shopping. That spending created a total estimated economic impact of more than $1.08 billion within the county. Tourism also supported approximately 8,520 local jobs and generated more than $287.2 million in wages and salaries during fiscal year 2023. Arts and culture can help expand that impact by giving visitors reasons to move beyond the beach, explore downtown areas, attend evening events and spend money with locally owned businesses. Tourism generates tax dollars St. Lucie County imposes a 5% Tourist Development Tax on qualifying short-term accommodations. Florida Department of Revenue records for 2026 list a combined tax rate of 12% on living and sleeping accommodations in St. Other taxable transactions generally are subject to a combined 7% rate. In 2023, taxes paid on visitor accommodations generated approximately $6.39 million in Tourist Development Tax collections. Visitors also generate sales tax revenue when they dine in restaurants, purchase merchandise, attend taxable attractions and make other purchases. The county’s 2023 economic impact report estimated that visitors produced a net tax benefit of approximately $9.07 million for St. Lucie County government after accounting for the cost of providing services to visitors. The same report estimated visitor-generated revenue saved local households approximately $406 per year in taxes. Tourism is not simply people arriving and taking photographs. Properly developed tourism helps pay the bills. How the Cultural Alliance can help The Cultural Alliance can serve as a connector between artists, cultural organizations, tourism officials, municipalities, hotels, restaurants and local businesses. Cultural tourism rarely succeeds when every organization markets itself in isolation. The Alliance can help develop cultural itineraries that combine galleries, performances, historic sites, public art, restaurants and shopping. A visitor attending Art Walk, for example, could also receive information about nearby dining, accommodations and weekend events. That turns one evening activity into a more complete visitor experience. The Alliance can also work with hotels and vacation rental operators to put cultural calendars, Art Walk information, gallery guides and event promotions directly in front of guests. Many visitors will attend cultural events when they know those events exist. The problem is often not a lack of things to do, but a lack of coordinated communication. The Alliance can also support artists through exhibition opportunities, calls for art, advocacy and professional connections. A successful cultural tourism economy requires a healthy creative sector. There is no cultural destination without artists, performers, writers, musicians and organizations capable of producing experiences worth traveling for. Investing in culture is investing in economic development Supporting arts and culture does not mean choosing creativity over economic growth. Creativity is part of economic growth. A successful cultural tourism strategy requires coordination among artists, cultural organizations, tourism officials, hotels, restaurants, municipalities and local businesses. Events should be marketed beyond the immediate community. Performances and exhibitions can be packaged with dining, lodging and shopping opportunities. Heritage trails and public art should be connected to nearby businesses and promoted as part of a complete visitor itinerary. Lucie Cultural Alliance can help lead that coordination. It represents the county’s cultural sector, promotes artists, publishes regional cultural content and creates partnerships designed to position St. Lucie County as an arts and cultural destination. The goal is not simply to attract more people. It is to give visitors more reasons to stay longer, explore more of the county and spend more money locally. Lucie County already has the stories, talent and cultural heritage. The opportunity is to connect those assets, market them consistently and present them as essential parts of the destination. Arts and culture do not compete with tourism. Linda Kloorfain is the marketing director of the St. Reach her at info@artstlucie.org . Your comment has been submitted.
