hero.headline: Woman surrenders 36 Border Collies rescued from Palm City hoarding case
hero.teaser: Paige O'Donnell has legally surrendered the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, clearing the way for the dogs to be adopted starting in September.
hero.body:
Paige O'Donnell has legally surrendered the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed Friday. Staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations so adopters receive clear information about any long-term needs before placement decisions are made. The dogs also will be prepared for spay and neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule.

Adoption applications will be available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's website and Facebook page beginning in September. Applicants will be highly vetted to ensure appropriate matches, and applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups also will be available beginning Sept. 1. To keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services, the shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time.

O'Donnell faces 72 charges in what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case it has ever seen. The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month. Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine, Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said. Fisher said some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur.

The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month. A WPTV investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe into the case.Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."WATCH BELOW: Deputies describe 'the filth' involved in rescuing 36 neglected dogsThe Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal.Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. hero.headline: Florida Tax Watch launches online tool showing Amendment 3 property tax impact by county
hero.teaser: Florida Tax Watch launched a Property Tax Resource Center that breaks down the proposed property tax measure by county and municipality, including St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties.
hero.body:
Florida Tax Watch launched a Property Tax Resource Center that allows voters to see the projected impact of Amendment 3 on property taxes by county and municipality across the state. Amendment 3 would expand the homestead exemption to $250,000 by 2028, which could cut local property taxes by nearly $46 billion over five years. The amendment needs 60% support to pass in November.

The website allows users to navigate to a state map, highlight any county, and see the projected five-year impact of Amendment 3 along with totals for each fiscal year. Users can also click through to see the impact on individual municipalities within each county. St. Lucie County ranks first in the state for millage and 16th in per capita property tax levies.

Palm Beach County is launching its own online tool in September where homeowners can see the direct impact the amendment would have on their individual property taxes. Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks said the tool is designed to give taxpayers a clear, personal picture of what a yes vote would mean for them. The online tool includes data for Palm Beach, St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River and Okeechobee counties.

hero.headline: Abandoned boats fill Wildcat Cove near Fort Pierce, creating safety hazards between nature preserves
hero.teaser: Abandoned and derelict boats are accumulating in Wildcat Cove off North Hutchinson Island in Fort Pierce, creating safety hazards and environmental concerns for residents and visitors. The area is located between two nature preserves and is popular for tubing and jet skiing.
hero.body:
Abandoned and derelict boats are filling up Wildcat Cove off North Hutchinson Island in Fort Pierce, creating safety hazards and environmental concerns for residents and visitors. Philipe Chibas, who lives nearby and runs Hot Reels Offshore Adventures, described the area as a "boat junkyard." "Looks like Water World out here," Chibas said. "I have to navigate through this minefield every time I go out with customers."

The boats are located between two nature preserves. The issue follows the city's implementation of a new ordinance limiting boats to anchoring in the water for 45 days before requiring them to be moved. However, Chibas said Wildcat Cove is outside the restricted zone, allowing the problem to persist. "Instead of solving the problem, they pushed the problem somewhere else," he said.

The area is also a popular spot for tubing and jet skiing, and residents are calling for the boats to be removed before an accident occurs. "They should be towed and destroyed," Chibas said. "You cant leave your car on 95." The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said it has issued several citations and is continuing to monitor the situation.

cards.headline: James Martin wins Democratic primary for Congressional District 21 by less than 1%, will face Brian Mast in November
cards.body:
Coast Guard veteran James Martin secured the Democratic nomination for Florida's 21st Congressional District Friday after capturing 50.4% of the vote compared to challenger Bernard Taylor's 49.6%, according to election results from NBC News. The narrow margin underscores the competitive nature of the Democratic race in a district that includes St. Lucie County, Martin County and portions of northern Palm Beach County. Martin will now face incumbent Republican Rep. Brian Mast in November's general election.

Taylor conceded the race Thursday night on social media, acknowledging the outcome while emphasizing the importance of democratic processes. "The voters have spoken, and while this isn't the outcome we hoped for, we respect their decision," Taylor wrote on X. "Democracy only works when we respect the voice of the people, even when the result isn't the one we wanted." Martin posted on Facebook Thursday evening that he was "honored to be the nominee" and congratulated Taylor on a "hard-fought race."

Rep. Brian Mast, an Army veteran who has represented the district since 2017, ran unopposed in the Republican primary. A Democrat has not represented this area of Florida in a decade. Both Martin and Mast bring military backgrounds to their campaigns, with Martin's Coast Guard service and Mast's Army experience potentially resonating with the significant veteran population throughout the Treasure Coast region.

Florida's 21st Congressional District spans a significant portion of the Treasure Coast, encompassing communities from northern Palm Beach County through Martin County and into St. Lucie County. With both major party nominees now confirmed, voters in St. Lucie, Martin and northern Palm Beach counties can expect an active campaign season as Martin challenges the incumbent Republican.

cards.headline: Two Fort Pierce women arrested after fake movie bill used to pay at Port St. Lucie restaurant
cards.teaser: Two Fort Pierce women were arrested after a counterfeit $100 bill with the words "FOR MOTION PICTURE PURPOSES" printed on it was used to pay for food and drinks at a Port St. Lucie restaurant.
cards.body:
Two Fort Pierce women were arrested after deputies said a counterfeit $100 bill was used to pay for food and drinks at a Port St. Lucie restaurant earlier this month. According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, three women went to a restaurant on St. Lucie West Boulevard on August 8 and ordered food and drinks. When it was time to pay, investigators said one of the women handed an employee a fake $100 bill that had the words "FOR MOTION PICTURE PURPOSES" printed on it.

Deputies said the women left the restaurant in a dark blue Dodge Charger. Patrol deputies later located the vehicle, and detectives with the Criminal Investigations Division assisted in the case. The investigation led to the arrest of Kamri Ashanti Reese, 24, of Fort Pierce. She faces charges of larceny, possession of a forged bank bill or note, and uttering a false bank bill, according to the sheriff's office. Investigators also arrested Kayla Reese, 25, of Fort Pierce, on a charge of possession of oxycodone without a prescription. The sheriff's office said both women are being held at the St. Lucie County Jail.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County community urges fire board to reinstate fired firefighters during packed meeting
cards.teaser: Nearly every public speaker at a St. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting Wednesday urged district leaders to reinstate three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations. The packed meeting lasted about three hours.
cards.body:
Nearly every public speaker at a St. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting Wednesday urged district leaders to reinstate three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations. The packed meeting lasted about three hours. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations.

Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said.

Fire Chief Jeff Lee addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. During the meeting, a motion was made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. The dispute is now in arbitration.

Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

cards.headline: Fired St. Lucie County firefighters question investigation transparency at district meeting
cards.teaser: Disciplined firefighters and community members urged the St. Lucie County Fire District to reinstate terminated firefighters at a meeting, alleging the investigation into hazing incidents was limited and mischaracterized.
cards.body:
At a St. Lucie County Fire District meeting, the community urged the district to reinstate the disciplined firefighters, alleging the investigation into hazing incidents was limited and mischaracterized. "Even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process," said Jordon Hutchinson, one of the terminated firefighters. The fire district disciplined five firefighters following an independent investigation into alleged hazing incidents. Videos surfaced that appeared to show the firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees.

Three firefighters were terminated, and now they are questioning the integrity of the investigation. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters are calling the disciplinary action retaliation for filing complaints against district leadership. At Wednesday's meeting, many residents argued that the investigation produced a limited report, with some allegations reviewed internally and others by independent investigators.

At the meeting, a motion was made to suspend the district chief and attorney, but the vote failed 4-1. The dispute has now moved to arbitration.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County fire board rejects motion to suspend fire chief and attorney over hazing controversy
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District board rejected a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district's attorney during a contentious meeting that included testimony from terminated firefighters. Four out of six commissioners voted against the suspension.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District board met to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation. After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it.

The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing. Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying, "It was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate." Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September.

hero.headline: Florida SNAP enrollment drops 22% as Trump-backed work requirements take effect
hero.body:
Enrollment in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program in Florida fell by more than 22% in a 12-month span as work requirements and other provisions of President Donald Trump's big beautiful bill take hold. The state's Department of Children and Families said in a statement that the decreasing number is reflective of the state's strong focus on advancing opportunities for Floridians and their families to achieve economic self-sufficiency. Nationwide, SNAP enrollment fell from 42.2 million in May 2025 to 36.6 million in May 2026, a drop of more than 13%.

The expanded SNAP work requirement now includes adults ages 55 to 64 and those with children ages 14 to 17. Many adults 54 and younger without minor children have long been required to work to get SNAP benefits. The new law requires most people who previously had been exempt from requirements to either work, volunteer or go to school to get benefits. Those 65 and older or with children younger than 14 remain exempt, as do those with health limitations. Some groups that had been exempted from the requirement, including homeless people, no longer are.

Paco Velez, the president and CEO of Feeding South Florida, said the 22% one-year enrollment drop in Florida is driven partly by immigrants who are in the U.S. legally but fear being targeted by Trump's immigration crackdown if they're seeking government benefits. Advocates say people are losing coverage because they miss deadlines or don't have the needed documentation handy, and that some state agencies that run the programs are overwhelmed trying to keep up with changes. Tia Fields, who analyzes social safety net policies at the advocacy group Invest in Louisiana, said the main reason she's seeing people lose coverage is not failure to meet work requirements but administrative paperwork.

The monthly SNAP benefit, which is delivered on debit cards that can be used only for groceries, is $344 per household on average. Children in households that receive the benefit can be automatically enrolled in free school lunch programs or in the SNAP for Women, Infants and Children program for low-income mothers, young children and expectant parents if they meet the other criteria. Some food banks have ramped up donations to try to meet a demand that has risen as SNAP rolls have declined, but advocates say that isn't expected to bridge the gap fully.
hero.article_text: Enrollment in the biggest federally funded food aid program in the U.S. dropped by more than 13% in a 12-month span — a decline far steeper than the government estimated as work requirements and other provisions of President Donald Trump's “big beautiful bill” take hold.Those losing coverage in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, include people who don't meet the tightening requirements to participate, and, advocates say, some who qualify for the help but are rejected because they miss deadlines or don't have the needed documentation handy. It's too early to tell exactly how many fall into each group.RELATED STORY | Judge rules government can't stop SNAP dollars from buying candy and sugary drinksIt's also unclear how many have lost coverage because some state agencies that run the programs are overwhelmed trying to keep up with changes. That was the case in Arizona, which saw the nation's largest enrollment drop.Tia Fields, who analyzes social safety net policies at the advocacy group Invest in Louisiana, said the main reason she's seeing people lose coverage is not failure to meet work requirements. “A lot of it is administrative paperwork,” she said.Proponents of welfare reform hope the roll reductions are driven by people earning too much to keep qualifying — a sign that policy changes are behaving as intended for a program they assert is riddled with fraud.“If there are people that are leaving the welfare rolls because they're working and they're moving forward,” said Rachel Sheffield, a research fellow at the conservative Heritage Foundation, which pushed for stricter requirements for SNAP, “that would be a step forward.”Arizona has had the steepest decline so far, with a 12-month drop of more than 50%, according to data compiled by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which runs SNAP. The decline was more than 20% in Georgia, Louisiana and Nevada — and in Florida, where the Department of Children and Families said in a statement that the decreasing number “is reflective of the state's strong focus on advancing opportunities for Floridians and their families to achieve economic self-sufficiency.”Eligibility requirements are tighteningSNAP helps more than 1 in 10 people in the U.S. Most of the beneficiaries have incomes below the poverty line. The monthly benefit, which is delivered on debit cards that can be used only for groceries, is $344 per household on average.Newly released federal data found SNAP enrollment fell from 42.2 million in May 2025 to 36.6 million in May, a drop of more than 13% in a year. The May data are preliminary and could be revised.Since 2010, the average number of monthly beneficiaries has been below 40 million for only two years — 2019 and 2020. The rolls started dropping after a recent peak of 43.3 million in October 2024. They've fallen much faster since implementation began last year for Trump’s “one big beautiful bill,” which cut taxes and overhauled social safety net programs.The expanded SNAP work requirement has now kicked in for most of the country, but it won’t begin in some places until next year.Many adults 54 and younger without minor children have long been required to work to get SNAP benefits. The new law requires most people who previously had been exempt from requirements to either work, volunteer or go to school to get benefits. It now includes those ages 55 to 64, and those with children ages 14 to 17. Those 65 and older or with children younger than 14 remain exempt, as do those with health limitations. Some other groups that had been exempted from the requirement — including homeless people — no longer are.In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected that the new requirements and other factors would push SNAP enrollment down over the next decade, falling below 34 million by 2036. But the nonpartisan office did not expect the drop to be as fast as it's been. By May, the number of people receiving the benefits was about as low as it was forecast to go in 2030.Experts expect another impact when states are required to pay part of the cost of benefits if their rate of payment errors — when recipients receive more or less than they should — is above 6%. Advocates for recipients say states may deny benefits to some people entirely rather than risk errors.The cost-sharing is scheduled to start in October 2027, though Congress has considered a delay.Changes have been hard to implement in ArizonaIn Arizona, enrollment plummeted by 55% from April 2025 to April 2026 — the biggest drop in the country, with more than 400,000 fewer people getting benefits now.The state said the drop was driven largely by the state's own struggles putting new federal requirements in place.RELATED STORY | SNAP benefits don't pay for rotisserie chicken. A bipartisan bill might change that“Implementing the federally mandated changes triggered unprecedented call volumes and administrative hurdles, including additional verification requirements, creating real barriers for applicants,” said Brett Bezio, a spokesman for the Arizona Department of Economic Security.Bezio said that hiring more staff members and introducing ways for people to submit their documents online have stemmed the enrollment drop in recent months as the state has reduced the chance for people who qualify to lose benefits.In Phoenix, LaDiamond Lopez lost her benefits in January, with officials telling her she needed more documentation about her income and household — something that's needed for officials to determine whether enrollees meet work requirements.She’s been skipping meals and some bill payments to ensure her children have enough to eat.In her quest to be reinstated, she had previous employers sign forms confirming she no longer worked for them and added her children — ages 3 and 9 — to her apartment lease. She expected payments to resume in August, but she doesn’t know if they’ll last.“I was approved at the end of May, but now they’re asking me for more documents,” she said. “It’s a panic.”Other factors could be driving down enrollmentThe Heritage Foundation's Sheffield says that some of the drop in SNAP use is likely a natural decline after peaks in the coronavirus pandemic era.Paco Velez, the president and CEO of Feeding South Florida, said the 22% one-year enrollment drop in Florida is driven partly by immigrants who are in the U.S. legally but fear being targeted by Trump's immigration crackdown if they're seeking government benefits.Invest in Louisiana's Fields said SNAP enrollment declines have broader consequences. For instance, children in households that receive the benefit can be automatically enrolled in free school lunch programs or in the SNAP for Women, Infants and Children program for low-income mothers, young children and expectant parents if they meet the other criteria.“What happens when that child can’t pay for lunch?” she asked.Some food banks have ramped up donations to try to meet a demand that they say has risen as SNAP rolls have declined. But that isn't expected to bridge the gap fully.“We’re very worried about it because we know that no other organization or program can replicate the scale and success of SNAP,” said Carolyn Vega, a policy analyst at the advocacy group Share Our Strength. “We know that schools can’t fill this gap. We know that food banks can’t fill this gap.”

hero.headline: Fort Pierce man arrested on eight burglary charges in Port St. Lucie Spanish Lakes community
hero.teaser: Herman Ray Nettles, 44, of Fort Pierce, is in the St. Lucie County Jail on eight counts of burglary of an unoccupied conveyance while unarmed on a $20,000 bond, stemming from incidents in the Spanish Lakes community in Port St. Lucie.
hero.body:
Herman Ray Nettles, 44, of Fort Pierce, was arrested on August 17 following multiple burglaries and attempted burglaries of vehicles in the Spanish Lakes One community in Port St. Lucie. St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office Patrol Operations Bureau deputies responded to multiple calls for service in the community. Working with Patrol Operations Bureau deputies and crime analysts, investigators developed and identified Nettles as a suspect.

St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office Deputy Martinez-Delgado, an off-duty officer, spotted Nettles traveling on U.S. Highway 1 in Port St. Lucie and notified 911. Patrol Operations Bureau deputies responded and detained Nettles before transporting him to the Criminal Investigations Division for further investigation. Probable cause was developed connecting Nettles to all eight incidents.

Nettles is in the St. Lucie County Jail as of August 21 on eight counts of burglary of an unoccupied conveyance while unarmed on a $20,000 bond. Being a law enforcement officer doesn't stop when the shift ends, said Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Deputy Martinez-Delgado's quick recognition and immediate action helped bring this suspect into custody, and I commend her for stepping up when it mattered.

cards.headline: Lauderhill man arrested in Treasure Coast Mall jewelry kiosk robbery worth over $22,000
cards.teaser: Dezmone Johnson, 25, of Lauderhill, is charged with robbery and grand theft after allegedly grabbing a tray of necklaces from Royal Jewelers kiosk at Treasure Coast Mall and fleeing the scene on July 20.
cards.body:
Dezmone Johnson, 25, of Lauderhill, was arrested after allegedly stealing more than $22,000 in jewelry from Royal Jewelers, a kiosk inside the Treasure Coast Mall in Jensen Beach, on July 20. Security video from the mall shows Johnson standing at the counter of the kiosk. He actually comes up and pretends to be a customer, engages with the clerk for a few minutes, said Chris Morales of the Martin County Sheriffs Office. According to Morales, Johnson walked away at one point before returning to ask for a closer look at the jewelry. The clerk brings out a tray of, let's say, seven or eight less expensive necklaces according to him, and he just grabs the tray and runs out, Morales said.

The necklaces are valued between $850 and $4,500 each, totaling more than $22,000 in stolen jewelry. Cameras outside the mall showed investigators the vehicle Johnson drove away in. We were able to get the tag from that vehicle, making it pretty easy for us. The vehicle came back to an address in Lauderhill, so down in Broward County, Morales said. Detectives visited a pawn shop near the Lauderhill address and stopped in to ask if Johnson was a customer. Lo and behold, the owner says, 'Yeah, he was just in here trying to pawn a few necklaces.' Again, making it pretty easy for our detectives, Morales said.

Johnson was arrested shortly afterward. Johnson is charged with robbery and grand theft. He spent a short time in the Broward County jail and is currently free on bond as he awaits trial. Morales said Johnson has a history of violence and has access to weapons in his criminal history.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce faces legal vacancy after Daniel McIntyre declines interim city attorney job
hero.body:
Fort Pierce will have no head city attorney beginning Sept. 11 after former St. Lucie County government attorney Daniel McIntyre turned down the city's offer to serve as interim municipal counsel. The Fort Pierce City Commission has called a special meeting for 9 a.m. Monday at City Hall to determine its next steps.

The commission voted 2-3 in June not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract for another year following controversy surrounding the handling of an employee disciplinary matter and claims the city attorney's office was difficult for employees and the public to deal with. Commissioner Broderick cast the lone no vote Aug. 10 when the other four commissioners decided to offer the interim job to McIntyre. Attorney John Anastasio, one-time counsel to former Port St. Lucie Mayor JoAnn Faiella, was the only other person brought to the commission for the interim appointment when McIntyre was selected.

The city is facing a number of potentially complicated legal matters in the upcoming months. A citizen has filed suit against the city over the handling of the leasing of the popular, city-owned Little Jim bar and restaurant property on North Hutchinson Island. Other legal matters could be coming over downtown waterfront projects Crabbys, Fishermans Wharf and Kings Landing.

The commission also is expected to consider Monday signing a contract to pay S. Renee Narlock Associates, a private headhunting firm from Tallahassee, up to $30,950 to recruit and screen applicants to succeed Hedges. The city also used the firm to hire Police Chief David Smith. According to the recruiting contract up for approval Monday, Narlock Associates predicts it could take 16 weeks before Hedges' successor is selected.

hero.headline: Indian River County works to extradite murder suspect arrested in West Virginia
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's Office is working to bring Matthew Allen Waggle, 32, back to Florida to face a first-degree murder charge in the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, outside her Vero Beach home in the 500 block of 1st Street on Aug. 16. U.S. Marshals deputies arrested Waggle on Aug. 19 at a motel in Dunbar, West Virginia, about six miles west of Charleston. Sheriff Eric Flowers announced at a press conference on Aug. 21 that the gun found near the scene belonged to the ex-wife of Waggle, who was also at the same motel where he was arrested.

Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewicz and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation. Kriskewicz, a hairdresser, had expressed concerns about Waggle to her coworkers at a hair salon. She had told her coworkers that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him and asked them to tell him she was not there.

Sheriff Flowers credited the Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle. He said without the Flock system, the office would not have been able to announce Waggle's arrest four days after the homicide. The sheriff said the system helped investigators piece together Waggle's movements after the shooting.

Waggle's ex-wife is still being questioned by detectives. Sheriff Flowers said investigators do not know the extent of her communication with Waggle or whether she knew his plans. She is not currently facing any charges. Indian River County detectives responded to a 911 call on Aug. 16 about a woman lying in the roadway at the 1st Street address.

cards.headline: Vero Beach hairdresser killed outside home, ex-boyfriend charged
cards.teaser: Matthew Waggle, 32, of Sebastian was arrested in West Virginia in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewicz, 52, outside her home on First Street in Vero Beach on Aug. 16.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced the arrest of Matthew Waggle in connection with the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewicz on First Street in Vero Beach early Sunday morning, Aug. 16. Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewicz and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said Kriskewicz had expressed concerns about Waggle to her coworkers at a hair salon. She had told her coworkers that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him and asked them to tell him she was not here. Flowers said Waggle was at the scene for 10 to 15 minutes at most and murdered Kriskewicz in cold blood in the street.

Waggle was found at a motel in West Virginia. Officials said the gun used in the shooting belonged to Waggle's ex-wife, who was at the same hotel where Waggle was arrested. Sheriff Flowers said investigators do not know the extent of their communication or whether she knew Waggle's plans. The ex-wife is still being questioned and is not currently facing any charges.

The sheriff credited the controversial Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle. “Without Flock, I’m not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia. So for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system,” Flowers said. Waggle was found at a motel in West Virginia, and officials said the gun used in the shooting belonged to Waggle’s ex-wife. “She was at the hotel, the same hotel that we got him at. So they were definitely in communication. We don’t know to what extent, what she knew. We don’t know if she knew his plans. All those are things that our detectives will be asking,” Flowers said. The sheriff added that Waggle’s ex-wife is still being questioned and is not currently facing any charges. hero.headline: Disciplined St. Lucie County firefighters challenge district investigation at public meeting
hero.teaser: Three terminated firefighters are questioning the integrity of an investigation into alleged hazing incidents at the St. Lucie County Fire District.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District faced community pressure Wednesday to reinstate five disciplined firefighters, with the terminated employees alleging the investigation into hazing incidents was limited and mischaracterized. Three firefighters were terminated and two were suspended following an independent investigation into alleged hazing incidents. Videos surfaced that appeared to show the firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees.

Jordon Hutchinson, one of the terminated firefighters, told the meeting that the disciplinary action was retaliation for filing complaints against district leadership. Many residents at the meeting argued that the investigation produced a limited report, with some allegations reviewed internally and others by independent investigators.

A motion was made to suspend the district chief and attorney, but the vote failed 4-1. The dispute has now moved to arbitration. Hutchinson said the firefighters are still trying to fix the process even after being fired.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office searches for missing man last seen Thursday morning
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is searching for Benton Doyle Tomlin, who was last seen at 2 a.m. Thursday. Authorities believe Tomlin may be endangered.

Tomlin is described as being 6 feet 1 inch tall, weighing 200 pounds, and having brown hair and brown eyes. The sheriff's office did not disclose where Tomlin was last seen.

Anyone who has seen Tomlin is asked to call 911 or contact Detective Corporal Drawdy at 772-462-3230. The sheriff's office released the missing person alert Friday morning.

The search for Tomlin comes as law enforcement agencies across the Treasure Coast continue to respond to missing person cases. The sheriff's office is asking the public for help locating Tomlin as quickly as possible.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Fire District board rejects motion to suspend chief and attorney
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District board voted down a motion to suspend the fire chief and district attorney after more than two hours of discussion about hazing allegations.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District board met Wednesday to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation.

After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it. The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing.

Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying it was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate. Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Stuart's Bathtub Beach
hero.teaser: Deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man who had swum more than 300 yards into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon.
hero.body:
Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life.

Deputy John Wilkes said the man was probably more than 300 yards from shore when he arrived on scene. Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was in a very distressed emotional state and advised that he was having relationship issues and issues with his direct family. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted.

Castoro said he built a rapport with the man and encouraged him to keep living. Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made.
hero.article_text: Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man faces five sexual activity with minor charges after SWAT operation
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz on Thursday morning after executing a search warrant at a residence in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. Vinz faces five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. Officers arrested Vinz without incident during the operation. The response drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Authorities said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry into the home.

Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024.

Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation and say they are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. Martinez said officers take cases involving children very seriously.

cards.teaser: Three terminated St. Lucie County firefighters are questioning the integrity of an investigation into alleged hazing incidents, calling the disciplinary action retaliation for filing complaints against district leadership.
cards.body:
At a St. Lucie County Fire District meeting on Wednesday, the community urged the district to reinstate the disciplined firefighters, alleging the investigation into hazing incidents was limited and mischaracterized. The fire district disciplined five firefighters following an independent investigation into alleged hazing incidents. Videos surfaced that appeared to show the firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees. Three firefighters were terminated, and two others were suspended.

The former firefighters are calling the disciplinary action retaliation for filing complaints against district leadership. At Wednesday's meeting, many residents argued that the investigation produced a limited report, with some allegations reviewed internally and others by independent investigators. A motion was made to suspend the district chief and attorney, but the vote failed 4-1. The dispute has now moved to arbitration.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County fire district board debates hazing allegations and leadership suspension
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire District board met Wednesday to discuss hazing allegations and the termination of three firefighters during a contentious meeting.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District board met Wednesday to discuss hazing allegations, the termination of three firefighters, and the suspension of two others during a contentious meeting. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, presented their case, accusing the fire chief and the district's attorney of retaliation. After more than two hours of discussion, commissioners called a motion to suspend the fire chief and the district attorney. The motion failed, with four out of six commissioners voting against it.

The situation stems from video footage released by the fire district showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which was described as hazing. Hutchinson and Baldwin denied the allegations, saying it was not hazing, but it was rather about inclusion, and that no one was hurt or coerced to participate. Commissioners approved a motion to continue the discussion at their next meeting in September.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on 5 sexual activity with minor charges after SWAT operation
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz early Thursday morning on five counts of sexual activity with a minor and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child after executing a search warrant at a home in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. Thursday and arrested Vinz without incident.

The SWAT operation drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry. Martinez said the devices are used for the safety of both officers and the individual during high-risk operations.

Vinz faces five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024.

Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation. Martinez said police take cases involving children very seriously. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending.

hero.body:

Investigators believe Waggle traveled by bus to Orlando and then used an Uber to reach Vero Beach, where he allegedly shot Kriskewic and left the scene just 15 minutes later using the same method of transportation.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle to her co-workers at a hair salon. She had actually told her co-workers out at the hair salon, If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him I'm not here, Flowers said during a news conference Thursday. He was there for 10, 15 minutes tops. He murdered her in cold blood in the street, Flowers said.

The sheriff credited the Flock license plate reader system for helping locate Waggle at a motel in West Virginia. Without Flock, I'm not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia. So for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system, Flowers said.

Waggle was found at a motel in West Virginia, and officials said the gun used in the shooting belonged to Waggle's ex-wife. She was at the hotel, the same hotel that we got him at. So they were definitely in communication. We don't know to what extent, what she knew. We don't know if she knew his plans. All those are things that our detectives will be asking, Flowers said. The sheriff added that Waggle's ex-wife is still being questioned and is not currently facing any charges.

hero.headline: Brightline station in downtown Stuart unlikely after Martin County denied federal funding
hero.body:
Martin County will not receive federal funding for a proposed Brightline station in downtown Stuart through the Intercity Passenger Rail Program, making the future of the project uncertain. The railroad bridge project in Stuart, a replacement for the century-old St.

U.S. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., who represents District 21 in the U.S. House of Representatives, said additional federal funding for a station is unlikely. Mast raised concerns about the structure of the proposed project, saying it is extremely problematic that the potential Brightline station would be entirely taxpayer-funded at the various levels, from federal all the way down to the local municipalities, with Brightline not putting anything into it. He said the company had no interest in examining whether they should build something less expensive.

John Dial, a mariner and owner of At the Helm Training, welcomed the bridge funding but expressed reservations about using public money for a private company's station. Christopher Vitale, the manager at the Old Colorado Inn, said a Brightline station would benefit the local economy and expressed hope that community leaders find another path forward. Jenna McGrew, a local resident, said federal tax dollars should go to things that help better the community, and a Brightline station would definitely help better the community.

Martin County released a statement saying it is pleased to see the announcement of federal funding for a Brightline station in Cocoa Beach, as well as additional federal funding awarded to the City of Stuart for the St. Lucie River Railroad Bridge. The county said it recognizes the importance of supporting and investment in transportation projects that benefit residents, strengthen local businesses and contribute to the continued economic vitality of the state. Tony Scozzafava, a resident, said he hopes the county can find an alternative approach to secure funding for the station.

cards.teaser: A motorist driving an SUV sustained traumatic injuries after colliding with a northbound Brightline train late Thursday morning near Southeast Dixie Highway and Southeast Crossrip Street in Hobe Sound.
cards.body:
A motorist driving an SUV sustained traumatic injuries after colliding with a northbound Brightline train late Thursday morning in Hobe Sound. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office and Fire Rescue, the crash happened near the intersection of Southeast Dixie Highway and Southeast Crossrip Street at around 11 a.m. The man driving the SUV was transported to the hospital.

Photos from the scene show multiple firefighters aiding the victim beside the SUV with heavy front-end damage while bystanders watched. Deputies advised motorists to avoid the area while investigators were at the scene. The train tracks were temporarily shut down but have since reopened. All lanes of traffic have reopened.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Bathtub Beach in Stuart
cards.teaser: Martin County deputies, lifeguards and marine units saved a man who was attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon.
cards.body:
Martin County deputies, lifeguards and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning and was probably 300-plus yards from the shore, according to Deputy John Wilkes.

Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was obviously in a very distressed emotional state and was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues and issues with his direct family. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living, relating over being fathers and discussing that it can be tough being a man and having emotions.

Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him and that there were a lot of people out there trying to help him, which changed his demeanor. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made.
cards.article_text: Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. hero.headline: Donalds pledges 20% insurance cut, backs data centers as Florida governor's race pivots to general election
hero.body:
Republican nominee Byron Donalds promised to reduce Florida property insurance costs by another 20% to 25% through regulatory changes and defended data center development as the governor's race shifts from the August primary to a November contest against Democratic nominee David Jolly. In a recent interview, Donalds outlined positions on property taxes, insurance, school vaccine requirements and data centers that now define the campaign.

Donalds supports Amendment 3, which would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for Floridians who establish permanent residency by the end of 2026. The measure would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. New residents would face a five-year phase-in before qualifying for the full exemption. A legislative financial analysis estimates the amendment would reduce local non-school property-tax revenue by nearly $5 billion in its first full fiscal year, with the recurring impact projected to approach $11.9 billion by the 2031-32 fiscal year. Donalds called the amendment a first step and suggested Florida should eventually consider a multi-tiered taxing system that treats counties differently based on property values and economic output. He did not spell out how the tiers would work or how local governments would replace lost revenue.

On insurance, Donalds said regulatory changes could push costs down another 20% to 25%. His ideas include changing the Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund, lowering reinsurance costs and making home-hardening grants more efficient. Donalds specifically pointed to the catastrophe fund's 25% cash buildup factor, which insurers pay on top of actuarially calculated premiums. He said the state could eliminate the charge or create a formula that turns it down when the fund has healthy reserves and raises it when the balance falls. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on 5 sexual activity with minor charges after SWAT operation
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested a 48-year-old man Thursday morning on multiple charges involving a minor after the department's SWAT team served a search warrant at a home in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. Officers took Virgil Jason Vinz into custody without incident around 6 a.m. He faces five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor.

Neighbors reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry. He said the devices are used for the safety of both officers and individuals during high-risk operations. Martinez said officers take any case involving a child very seriously but are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active.

Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024.

Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation.

hero.headline: Sebastian man arrested in West Virginia for Vero Beach homicide after Flock license plate readers track multi-state flight
hero.body:
Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, of Sebastian was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel and faces a first-degree murder charge in the fatal shooting of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, a Vero Beach hairdresser, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. The arrest ended a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and began life-saving measures. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that Kriskewic had recently ended things with him. Kriskewic had told her co-workers that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him. Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from West Virginia to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence after being dropped off around the corner, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area.

After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators. The sheriff's office real-time crime center tracked Waggle's movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. U.S. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle's ex-wife.

Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic's body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night. Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday's announcement. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges in Indian River County.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County fire board meeting draws calls to reinstate three fired firefighters over hazing allegations
cards.teaser: Community members packed a Wednesday board meeting to support three firefighters fired following a hazing investigation. Nearly every public speaker urged the St. Lucie County Fire District board to bring the men back.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting Wednesday turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations. The packed meeting lasted about three hours, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them.

The St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others last month over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired.

Fire Chief Jeff Lee told the crowd he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. Lee acknowledged the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. The dispute is now in arbitration. A motion to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney failed during the meeting. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting.

The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

hero.headline: SUV driver hospitalized after collision with Brightline train in Hobe Sound
hero.body:
An SUV collided with a northbound Brightline train Thursday morning in Hobe Sound, sending the driver to the hospital with traumatic injuries. The crash occurred just before 11 a.m. near the intersection of Southeast Dixie Highway and Southeast Crossrip Street.

Martin County Fire Rescue crews transported the man to a local hospital. Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to the scene and are working to determine the cause of the collision.

All train tracks in the area have been reopened following the incident. Martin County Fire Rescue and the Martin County Sheriff's Office handled the emergency response.

The proper investigative agencies have been notified of the collision. The incident marks another collision between a vehicle and Brightline trains that run through Martin County communities.

The man driving the SUV sustained traumatic injuries and was taken to a local hospital. Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies also responded to the scene, and are working to determine the cause of the collision. All train tracks in the area have since been reopened following the incident.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies rescue man attempting suicide at Bathtub Beach in Stuart
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and marine units rescued a man who swam hundreds of yards into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon after he called a suicide hotline saying he intended to end his life.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, lifeguards, and marine units rescued a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had made the final decision to end his life.

The man had already swum approximately 300 yards from shore when Deputy John Wilkes arrived on scene. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. Sergeant Nicholas Castoro said the man was in a very distressed emotional state and advised that he was having relationship issues and issues with his direct family. The man told deputies the ocean was peaceful for him and he wanted to swim out until he got tired.

Castoro built a rapport with the man and encouraged him to keep living, relating over being fathers. Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him and changed his demeanor, deciding not to end his life that day. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made.
cards.article_text: Martin County deputies, lifeguards, and marine units worked together to save a man attempting to end his life by swimming far out into the ocean at Bathtub Beach in Stuart on Sunday afternoon. Deputies were dispatched to the beach after receiving a call from the suicide hotline, where the man said he had "made the final decision to end his life." "My biggest thing was stopping him from continuing to swim further into the ocean," Deputy John Wilkes said. "Because once I arrived on scene, they had already swam out to them and if I had to put a number on it, they were probably 300-plus yards from the shore." Sergeant Nicholas Castoro described the man’s emotional state. "He was obviously in a very distressed emotional state; he was in a lot of need. He advised that he was having some relationship issues. Issues with his direct family," Castoro said. Wilkes explained how the training the sheriff's office requires helped deputies during the rescue. "Crisis intervention training, which helps us learn how to kind of deal with somebody that’s dealing with a mental health crisis or substance abuse or something along those lines, definitely helped us all that day," Wilkes said. The man continued swimming out into the ocean with no intention of returning. Lifeguards on duty tried to save him, but he resisted. "I think he kind of said that the ocean was peaceful for him, and he just said he wanted to swim out until he got tired," Castoro said. Before deputies helped the man get on the boat, Castoro said he built a rapport with him and encouraged him to keep living. "We were able to relate over being fathers, and you know that it can be tough being a man and having emotions, especially expressing those emotions or seeking the help that you need," Castoro said. "Having children and pushing on for our children, and hopefully that’ll get him through his time of need." Wilkes said the man began to realize the support around him. "He would kind of look back at me and realize, 'Wow, there’s a lot of people out here trying to help me right now,' and I think that’s what really is what changed his demeanor and said this is the wrong decision, I’m not doing this today," Wilkes said. After the man decided to get on the boat, he was transported to the hospital, where he was medically cleared in the emergency room. He was later placed under a law enforcement Baker Act due to some of the statements he made. hero.headline: Florida school camera lawsuits face dismissals as judges side with automated enforcement systems
hero.body:
Legal challenges to automated school bus and school zone cameras that have generated more than 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in fines across Florida are hitting roadblocks as judges dismiss cases and rule against drivers contesting tickets. Miami-based Attorney Gino Moreno filed three lawsuits last year after drivers hit with $225 school bus camera fines had no way to challenge their citations because the cameras started operating without proper due process in place. Since then, a judge dismissed his federal case in Polk County, a revised complaint remains pending in Miami-Dade, and a Hillsborough County case filed on behalf of client Stanley Shultz awaits a decision on whether it will move forward.

Shultz, who lives in Plant City, was fined for illegally passing a school bus even though video from his citation shows the bus warning lights never flashed. Shultz appealed the fine, but a judge in Tallahassee upheld it despite state law requiring appeals must be heard by local hearing officers. Shultz is now accusing the county of not following state rules for appeal hearings. Legal questions extend beyond school buses to school speed zone cameras, with drivers fined when school was not in session or when signs directing them to slow down when flashing never flashed.

Questions have also emerged about the camera devices themselves. The radar inside the cameras, which state law requires to be approved by the state, is not approved. The state maintains it is exempt. Attorney Ira Karmelin with The Ticket Clinic has successfully used that argument to get school speed zone tickets thrown out, but judges are now starting to side with the state claim of exemption, even though the exemption refers to a radar design, not the device itself.

Since the cameras began operating in Florida, they have generated well over 1 million citations and tens of millions of dollars in paid fines as of earlier this year. While these legal challenges continue to hit roadblocks, judges have left the door open for appeals or new legal arguments. Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp have been tracking the problems with these automated school cameras for nearly three years.
